documents.t: Java’s Executors class provides several factory methods to create various types of thread pools: public static ExecutorService newSingleThreadExecutor() public static ExecutorService newFixedThreadPool(int nThreads) public static ExecutorService newCachedThreadPool() public static ScheduledExecutorService newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() public static ScheduledExecutorService newScheduledThreadPool(int corePoolSize) These convenience methods simplify thread pool creation, but they do not allow fine-tuning. Using Executors to create thread pools is generally discouraged due to potential risks, such as resource exhaustion. The official guidance is to use ThreadPoolExecutor directly, enabling full control over pool configurations, ensuring stability under varying load conditions.

public class ThreadDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { ExecutorService es = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); } } Why it's discouraged: Creating a thread pool this way can lead to issues like uncontrolled resource usage. Best practice: use ThreadPoolExecutor instead.

Java's ThreadPoolExecutor is a cornerstone of concurrent programming. It provides a high-performance, versatile API for managing threads and handling tasks, but it requires careful configuration to prevent resource wastage, improve system responsiveness, and enhance maintainability.

The ThreadPoolExecutor manages thread allocation, scaling, and task queueing while optimizing thread lifecycle to minimize system overhead. Here is a basic textual model of a ThreadPoolExecutor lifecycle and memory model: +-----------------------------+ | Task Queue | | (BlockingQueue<Runnable>) | +------------+----------------+ | +-----------------v-----------------+ | | | ThreadPoolExecutor | | | +----------------+------------------+ | +----------------------+--------------------+ | Worker Threads | | +-----------------------------------+ | | | Worker Thread 1 | | | |-----------------------------------| | | | Worker Thread 2 | | | |-----------------------------------| | | | Worker Thread N | | +-------------------------------------------+ Worker Threads: Execute tasks within a controlled environment. Task Queue: Holds tasks awaiting execution, preventing unnecessary thread creation. ThreadPoolExecutor: Controls the execution strategy, pool scaling, and task rejection policies.

To avoid risks, use ThreadPoolExecutor directly for creating thread pools: public class ThreadDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { ExecutorService es = new ThreadPoolExecutor(1, 1, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>(10), Executors.defaultThreadFactory(), new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy()); } }

The ThreadPoolExecutor relies on several key configuration parameters: corePoolSize: Minimum number of threads in the pool. maximumPoolSize: Maximum threads allowed in the pool. keepAliveTime: The time a thread can remain idle before termination if beyond corePoolSize. workQueue: Queue holding tasks before they are assigned to threads. Best Practice: Choose configuration values based on workload type and system capacity.​

The methods newSingleThreadExecutor(), newFixedThreadPool(int nThreads), and newCachedThreadPool() all internally use ThreadPoolExecutor. Below are the source code implementations from JDK 8: public static ExecutorService newSingleThreadExecutor() { return new FinalizableDelegatedExecutorService( new ThreadPoolExecutor(1, 1, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>()) ); } public static ExecutorService newFixedThreadPool(int nThreads) { return new ThreadPoolExecutor(nThreads, nThreads, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>()); } public static ExecutorService newCachedThreadPool() { return new ThreadPoolExecutor(0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new SynchronousQueue<Runnable>()); } All three methods use ThreadPoolExecutor but provide different default configurations. These static methods abstract parameters, which can lead to undesired behaviors under high loads.

When creating thread pools with ThreadPoolExecutor, initializing parameters must be specified. One of its constructors takes the following parameters: public ThreadPoolExecutor(int corePoolSize, int maximumPoolSize, long keepAliveTime, TimeUnit unit, BlockingQueue<Runnable> workQueue, ThreadFactory threadFactory, RejectedExecutionHandler handler)

corePoolSize: Number of threads to keep in the pool. maximumPoolSize: Maximum number of threads allowed. keepAliveTime: Time limit for idle threads over corePoolSize before termination. unit: Unit of time for keepAliveTime. workQueue: Queue to hold tasks before execution. threadFactory: Factory for creating threads, usually Executors.defaultThreadFactory(). handler: Policy for handling tasks when the pool reaches its limit.

Choosing the Right Queue: SynchronousQueue: No internal capacity, ideal for transient spikes. LinkedBlockingQueue: Unbounded, suitable for long-running processes. ArrayBlockingQueue: Fixed size, optimal for bounded workloads. Note: Select a queue type aligned with task load, duration, and resource availability.

If thread count < corePoolSize, a new thread is created for each task. If thread count >= corePoolSize, tasks are added to the task queue. If the queue is full and thread count < maximumPoolSize, a new thread is created. If thread count >= maximumPoolSize, the handler policy determines the behavior. Note: These relationships vary with the type of queue (bounded or unbounded). Unbounded queues will prevent maximum thread creation from being reached.

The workQueue holds pending tasks that await execution. Different queue types handle tasks differently: SynchronousQueue: A direct hand-off mechanism with no capacity. If no thread is immediately available, a new one is created or the task is rejected based on maximumPoolSize. LinkedBlockingQueue: An unbounded queue. When tasks exceed corePoolSize, they are added to the queue instead of creating new threads. Warning: Unbounded growth may exhaust memory if tasks are generated faster than processed.

Efficient scaling balances resource use against workload demands. Consider using dynamic scaling mechanisms for responsive systems. Recommended Scaling:​ FixedThreadPool: When task load and timing are predictable. CachedThreadPool: For unpredictable or short-lived task loads.

When the pool and queue are full, the handler parameter specifies a strategy to handle tasks. Java provides four built-in policies: DiscardOldestPolicy: Removes the oldest task in the queue to accommodate the new task. CallerRunsPolicy: Executes the task in the caller thread if the pool is busy, providing a backpressure mechanism. DiscardPolicy: Silently discards the task without further action. AbortPolicy: Throws an exception to signal that the pool is at capacity. Note: Customize RejectedExecutionHandler based on workload characteristics. Expecially for applications where resilience is critical, consider implementing a custom rejection handler or using CallerRunsPolicy to limit load. Proper configuration can prevent issues like out-of-memory errors. RejectedExecutionHandler customHandler = new RejectedExecutionHandler() { public void rejectedExecution(Runnable r, ThreadPoolExecutor executor) { System.out.println("Task rejected: " + r.toString()); // custom logic for rejected task } };

documents.t: Monitoring thread and queue activity is essential for real-time scaling and troubleshooting. Use the following tools and approaches: JMX (Java Management Extensions): For real-time metrics on threads, tasks, and system load. Thread Pool Executor's getPoolSize and getQueue().size() Methods: To track runtime capacity and pending task counts.

Backpressure handling in high-demand environments prevents overloads by controlling the flow of tasks: Rejection Policies: Define fallback strategies for rejected tasks. Queue Sizing: Set boundaries on task input rate. Diagram: Dynamic Task Flow and Backpressure​ Client Requests | +----v----+ Backpressure Control | Task |--------------------+ | Queue | | +---------+ | | | +------v-------+ | | Thread | | | Pool | | +--------------+----------------+

import java.util.concurrent.*; public class OptimizedThreadPoolExecutor { public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. Configure core parameters with scaling strategy ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, // core pool size 10, // maximum pool size 30, // keep-alive time TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keep-alive time unit new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), // task queue type new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // rejection policy ); // 2. Simulate task submission for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { executor.submit(new Task(i)); } executor.shutdown(); } static class Task implements Runnable { private final int taskId; Task(int taskId) { this.taskId = taskId; } @Override public void run() { System.out.println("Executing Task " + taskId); try { Thread.sleep(500); // Simulate work } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } }

Summary: Use ThreadPoolExecutor directly with appropriately sized pools, tailored queue types, and effective rejection policies to ensure optimal, safe performance. Mastering ThreadPoolExecutor for complex, production-grade applications requires an understanding of core parameters, workload patterns, and monitoring needs. These best practices are intended to improve performance, efficiency, and system resilience in multithreaded environments.

documents.t: Monitoring and tuning Linux system performance is crucial for maintaining the health and efficiency of your infrastructure. Command line tools like top, htop, iotop, sar, ps, free, vmstat, and netstat provide powerful capabilities for analyzing and optimizing system performance. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using these tools, covering various scenarios such as checking CPU and memory usage, monitoring processes, and troubleshooting real production issues.
To check CPU usage, use the top command: top This command displays real-time CPU and memory usage, along with a list of running processes.
To check memory usage, use the free command: free -h This command displays the total, used, and free memory in a human-readable format.
To check disk I/O, use the iostat command: iostat -x 1 This command displays detailed I/O statistics, including read and write rates.
To check network traffic, use the iftop command: iftop -i eth0 This command displays real-time network traffic on the eth0 interface.
To list all running processes, use the ps command: ps aux This command displays a detailed list of all running processes.

To check the status of a specific process, use the ps command with the process ID (PID): ps -p <PID> -o pid,ppid,cmd,%cpu,%mem,state This command displays the status of the process with the specified PID.
To kill a process, use the kill command with the process ID (PID): kill <PID> This command sends a termination signal to the process with the specified PID.
To monitor system performance in real-time, use the top command: top This command provides a dynamic view of system resources and running processes.
To monitor system performance with a more user-friendly interface, use htop: htop This command provides a colorful and interactive view of system resources and running processes.
To monitor disk I/O in real-time, use the iotop command: iotop This command displays real-time disk I/O statistics for running processes.
To collect and report system activity, use the sar command: sar -u 1 5 This command collects CPU usage statistics every second for 5 seconds.
To identify processes causing high CPU usage, use top or htop: top Sort processes by CPU usage by pressing P.
To identify processes causing high memory usage, use top or htop: top Sort processes by memory usage by pressing M.
To identify processes causing high disk I/O, use iotop: iotop This command displays real-time disk I/O statistics for running processes.
To diagnose network latency, use ping and traceroute: ping google.com traceroute google.com These commands help identify network latency and routing issues.

Monitoring and tuning Linux system performance is essential for maintaining the health and efficiency of your infrastructure. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use command line tools like top, htop, iotop, sar, ps, free, vmstat, and netstat to analyze and optimize system performance.

documents.t: Network analysis is a critical skill for system administrators and network engineers. Command line tools like ping, traceroute, netstat, tcpdump, nmap, iftop, and wireshark provide powerful capabilities for monitoring, diagnosing, and troubleshooting network issues. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using these tools, covering various scenarios such as capturing and filtering network traffic, displaying network statistics, and diagnosing network issues.
To check connectivity to a host, use the ping command: ping google.com This command sends ICMP echo requests to the specified host and displays the response time.
To trace the route to a host, use the traceroute command: traceroute google.com This command shows the path packets take to reach the specified host.
To display network statistics and active connections, use the netstat command: netstat -a This command displays all active connections and listening ports.
To test network connections and transfer data, use the nc (netcat) command: nc -zv google.com 80 This command checks if port 80 is open on google.com.
To capture and analyze network traffic, use the tcpdump command: tcpdump -i eth0 This command captures all traffic on the eth0 interface.
To capture and analyze network traffic with a graphical interface, use wireshark: wireshark This tool provides advanced filtering and analysis capabilities.
To scan for open ports and services on a host, use the nmap command: nmap 192.168.1.1 This command scans the specified IP address for open ports and services.
To monitor network traffic in real-time, use the iftop command: iftop -i eth0 This command displays real-time network traffic on the eth0 interface.
To filter tcpdump output, use grep: tcpdump -i eth0 | grep "HTTP" This command filters tcpdump output to show only HTTP traffic.
To process netstat output, use awk: netstat -an | awk '/:80 / {print $5}' This command extracts the IP addresses of connections on port 80.
To process nmap output, use sed: nmap 192.168.1.1 | sed -n '/open/p' This command filters nmap output to show only open ports.
To capture and analyze HTTP traffic, use tcpdump with port filtering: tcpdump -i eth0 port 80
To monitor real-time traffic on a specific interface, use iftop: iftop -i eth0
To diagnose network issues, use a combination of ping, traceroute, and tcpdump: ping google.com traceroute google.com tcpdump -i eth0 host google.com

Network analysis is a critical skill for maintaining and troubleshooting network infrastructure. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use command line tools like ping, traceroute, netstat, tcpdump, nmap, iftop, and wireshark to monitor, diagnose, and troubleshoot network issues.

documents.t: Docker is a powerful tool for application development, enabling developers to package applications and their dependencies into containers. This article provides a comprehensive guide to best practices for using Docker in application development, covering various scenarios such as communicating among containers, mounting local files/folders, and managing multi-container applications.

To run a Docker container, use the docker run command: docker run -d --name my-container my-image This command runs a container in detached mode (-d) with the name my-container using the image my-image.
To build a Docker image from a Dockerfile, use the docker build command: docker build -t my-image . This command builds an image with the tag my-image using the Dockerfile in the current directory.

Containers can communicate with each other using Docker networks. By default, Docker creates a bridge network that allows containers to communicate with each other. Example​ To create a network and run two containers on the same network: docker network create my-network docker run -d --name container1 --network my-network my-image1 docker run -d --name container2 --network my-network my-image2 Containers container1 and container2 can now communicate with each other using their container names as hostnames.

To mount local files or folders into a Docker container, use the -v or --volume option: docker run -d --name my-container -v /path/to/local/folder:/path/in/container my-image This command mounts the local folder /path/to/local/folder into the container at /path/in/container.

Docker networks allow containers to communicate with each other securely and efficiently. You can create custom networks and attach containers to them. Example​ To create a custom network and attach containers: docker network create my-network docker run -d --name container1 --network my-network my-image1 docker run -d --name container2 --network my-network my-image2 Containers container1 and container2 can now communicate with each other using their container names as hostnames.

To run a Spring Boot application that connects to a PostgreSQL database, follow these steps: Create a Docker Network: Create a Docker network for the containers to communicate. docker network create my-network Run PostgreSQL Container: Run a PostgreSQL container on the network. docker run -d --name postgres --network my-network -e POSTGRES_USER=user -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password -e POSTGRES_DB=mydb postgres:13 Build Spring Boot Application Image: Build the Docker image for the Spring Boot application. docker build -t spring-boot-app . Run Spring Boot Application Container: Run the Spring Boot application container on the same network. docker run -d --name spring-boot-app --network my-network -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/mydb -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=user -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=password spring-boot-app In this setup, the Spring Boot application connects to the PostgreSQL database using the JDBC URL jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/mydb, where postgres is the hostname of the PostgreSQL container.

Use Minimal Base Images: Use minimal base images that contain only the necessary components. Regularly Update Dependencies: Regularly update dependencies to ensure security patches are applied. Scan for Vulnerabilities: Use tools like docker scan to scan images for vulnerabilities. Avoid Storing Secrets: Avoid storing secrets in Dockerfiles. Use environment variables or secret management tools.
Limit Resource Usage: Use resource limits to prevent containers from consuming excessive resources. Use Ephemeral Containers: Use ephemeral containers that can be easily replaced or updated.

Enable Logging: Enable logging for containers to track application behavior and diagnose issues. Monitor Container Performance: Monitor container performance and resource usage to ensure optimal operation.

In scenarios where your application needs to handle flow control and backpressure, you can use environment variables to configure the behavior. Example​ docker run -d --name my-app --network my-network -e MAX_CONNECTIONS=100 -e BACKPRESSURE_THRESHOLD=50 my-image

documents.t: For complex applications with multiple containers, use Docker Compose to define and manage multi-container applications. Example docker-compose.yml​ version: '3.8' services: postgres: image: postgres:13 environment: POSTGRES_USER: user POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password POSTGRES_DB: mydb networks: - my-network spring-boot-app: image: spring-boot-app environment: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/mydb SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: user SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: password networks: - my-network networks: my-network: driver: bridge To start the application, run: docker-compose up -d

curl is a powerful command-line tool used for transferring data with URLs. It supports a wide range of protocols, including HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and more. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using curl, covering various scenarios such as checking if an URL is alive, downloading files, making HTTP GET/POST requests, handling authentication, and dealing with HTTPS certificates.

To check if an URL is alive, you can use the -I (or --head) option to send a HEAD request: curl -I https://example.com This command will return the HTTP headers without downloading the content, allowing you to quickly check if the URL is accessible.
documents.s: Check if an URL is Alive

documents.t: To download a file from a URL, simply use the curl command followed by the URL: curl -O https://example.com/file.zip The -O option saves the file with the same name as the remote file. If you want to save the file with a different name, use the -o option: curl -o myfile.zip https://example.com/file.zip
To make an HTTP GET request, use the curl command followed by the URL: curl https://example.com/api/resource

To make an HTTP POST request with a JSON payload, use the -X POST option and specify the JSON data using the -d option: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"key1":"value1", "key2":"value2"}' https://example.com/api/resource
To use HTTP Basic Authentication, use the -u option to specify the username and password: curl -u username:password https://example.com/api/resource
To use Bearer Token Authentication, use the -H option to set the Authorization header: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" https://example.com/api/resource
To use HTTPS with a client certificate, use the --cert and --key options: curl --cert client.crt --key client.key https://example.com/api/resource
To ignore HTTPS certificate validation (not recommended for production), use the -k (or --insecure) option: curl -k https://example.com/api/resource
To send custom headers, use the -H option: curl -H "X-Custom-Header: value" https://example.com/api/resource
To follow HTTP redirects, use the -L (or --location) option: curl -L https://example.com/redirect
To get verbose output, use the -v (or --verbose) option: curl -v https://example.com/api/resource
To set a timeout for the request, use the --connect-timeout and --max-time options: curl --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 https://example.com/api/resource

curl is a versatile and powerful tool for interacting with web services and downloading files from the command line. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use curl for a wide range of tasks, from simple URL checks to complex HTTP requests with authentication and custom headers.

documents.t: The awk command is a powerful text processing tool in Unix-like operating systems. It is particularly useful for manipulating and analyzing structured text data, such as log files, CSV files, and other tabular data. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using the awk command, covering various scenarios such as printing lines, field manipulation, pattern matching, and combining awk with other commands using pipelines.
To print all lines from a file, use the following command: awk '{print}' filename.txt
To specify a custom field separator, use the -F option: awk -F, '{print}' filename.csv
To print specific fields, use the $ notation: awk '{print $1, $3}' filename.txt This command prints the first and third fields of each line.
To print lines that match a specific pattern, use the ~ operator: awk '/pattern/ {print}' filename.txt
To use conditional statements, use the if statement: awk '{if ($1 > 10) print $0}' filename.txt This command prints lines where the first field is greater than 10.
To use loops, use the for loop: awk '{for (i=1; i<=NF; i++) print $i}' filename.txt This command prints each field on a new line.
To use arrays, use the array[index] notation: awk '{array[$1]++} END {for (i in array) print i, array[i]}' filename.txt This command counts the occurrences of each value in the first field.
To combine awk with grep, use a pipeline: grep "pattern" filename.txt | awk '{print $2}' This command prints the second field of lines that match the pattern.
To combine awk with sed, use a pipeline: sed 's/old/new/g' filename.txt | awk '{print $1}' This command replaces old with new in each line and then prints the first field.
To combine awk with find, use a pipeline: find /path/to/search -name "*.log" | awk -F/ '{print $NF}' This command prints the base name of each .log file found by find.
To sum the values in a column, use the + operator: awk '{sum += $1} END {print sum}' filename.txt This command sums the values in the first column.
To calculate the average of a column, use the + operator and divide by the number of lines: awk '{sum += $1} END {print sum/NR}' filename.txt This command calculates the average of the first column.
To format the output, use the printf function: awk '{printf "%-10s %s\n", $1, $2}' filename.txt This command formats the first field to be left-aligned with a width of 10 characters.

The awk command is a versatile and powerful tool for text processing and data analysis. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use awk for a wide range of tasks, from simple text manipulation to complex data processing and analysis.

documents.s: Best Practices of Using the find Command

documents.t: The find command is a powerful tool in Unix-like operating systems for searching files and directories based on various criteria such as name, type, size, owner, date, and more. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using the find command, covering various scenarios such as finding files by name, content, owner, date, and combining find with other commands using pipelines.
To find files by name, use the -name option: find /path/to/search -name "filename.txt"
To find files using a wildcard pattern, use the -name option with wildcards: find /path/to/search -name "*.log"
To find files containing specific content, use the -exec option with grep: find /path/to/search -type f -exec grep -l "search_string" {} \;
By default, find searches in all subdirectories. You can specify the starting directory: find /path/to/search -name "filename.txt"
To find files owned by a specific user, use the -user option: find /path/to/search -user username

To find files modified within a specific time range, use the -mtime option: find /path/to/search -mtime -7 # Files modified in the last 7 days find /path/to/search -mtime +7 # Files modified more than 7 days ago
documents.s: Find Files by Date and Time

documents.t: To perform an action on the found files, use xargs: find /path/to/search -name "*.log" | xargs rm
To search for files containing specific content, use grep with find: find /path/to/search -type f -exec grep -l "search_string" {} \;
To process the output of find with awk, use a pipeline: find /path/to/search -name "*.txt" | awk '{print $1}'
To find and delete files, use the -delete option: find /path/to/search -name "*.bak" -delete
To find and move files, use the -exec option with mv: find /path/to/search -name "*.log" -exec mv {} /path/to/destination/ \;
To find and copy files, use the -exec option with cp: find /path/to/search -name "*.txt" -exec cp {} /path/to/destination/ \;

The find command is a versatile and powerful tool for searching files and directories based on various criteria. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use find for a wide range of tasks, from simple file searches to complex operations involving multiple commands and pipelines.

The command find /path/to/search -type f -exec grep -l "search_string" {} \; can be rewritten using xargs. The xargs command is useful for building and executing command lines from standard input. Here’s how you can rewrite the command using xargs: Using xargs to rewrite the find command with -exec can make your command more efficient and easier to read. By leveraging xargs, you can handle large numbers of files more effectively and streamline your command-line operations. find /path/to/search -type f | xargs grep -l "search_string"

find /path/to/search -type f: This part of the command finds all files (-type f) in the specified directory and its subdirectories. | xargs grep -l "search_string": The | (pipe) symbol passes the list of files found by find to xargs. xargs then constructs and executes the grep command for each file, searching for the specified string ("search_string") and printing the names of files that contain the string (-l option).

Efficiency: xargs can handle a large number of files more efficiently than the -exec option, especially when dealing with a large number of files. Simplification: The xargs version is often simpler and more concise.

Suppose you want to find all files in the /var/log directory that contain the string "error". You can use the following command: find /var/log -type f | xargs grep -l "error" This command will output the names of all files in the /var/log directory and its subdirectories that contain the string "error".

The {} in the command find /path/to/search -name "*.log" -exec mv {} /path/to/destination/ \; is a placeholder that represents the current file being processed by the find command. Let's break down the command and understand the role of {}. The {} placeholder in the find command with -exec is a powerful feature that allows you to dynamically insert the current file path into the command being executed. This makes it easy to perform operations on each file found by find, such as moving, copying, or deleting files.

find /path/to/search -name "*.log" -exec mv {} /path/to/destination/ \; find /path/to/search -name "*.log": This part of the command searches for all files in the /path/to/search directory and its subdirectories that match the pattern *.log. -exec mv {} /path/to/destination/ \;: This part of the command executes the mv command for each file found by find. {}: This placeholder is replaced by the full path of the current file found by find. For example, if find finds a file named example.log in the directory /path/to/search/subdir, {} will be replaced by /path/to/search/subdir/example.log. /path/to/destination/: This is the destination directory where the files will be moved. \;: This is the terminator for the -exec command. It tells find that the command is complete.

Suppose you have the following directory structure: /path/to/search/ ├── file1.log ├── file2.log └── subdir/ └── file3.log Running the command: find /path/to/search -name "*.log" -exec mv {} /path/to/destination/ \; will result in the following actions: find will locate file1.log, file2.log, and subdir/file3.log. For each file found, find will execute the mv command: mv /path/to/search/file1.log /path/to/destination/ mv /path/to/search/file2.log /path/to/destination/ mv /path/to/search/subdir/file3.log /path/to/destination/ After the command completes, all .log files will be moved to the /path/to/destination/ directory.

find Man Page GNU findutils Documentation xargs Man Page grep Man Page awk Man Page By following these best practices, you can leverage the find command to its full potential and efficiently manage your file searches and operations from the command line.

documents.s: Best Practices of Using the sed Command

documents.t: The sed command is a powerful stream editor for filtering and transforming text in Unix-like operating systems. It is particularly useful for performing search-and-replace operations, deleting lines, and modifying text files. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using the sed command, covering various scenarios such as substitution, pattern matching, in-place editing, and combining sed with other commands using pipelines.
To replace a pattern with another string, use the s command: sed 's/old/new/' filename.txt This command replaces the first occurrence of old with new in each line.
To delete lines that match a pattern, use the d command: sed '/pattern/d' filename.txt This command deletes all lines containing the pattern.
To print lines that match a pattern, use the p command: sed -n '/pattern/p' filename.txt This command prints all lines containing the pattern.
To match patterns using regular expressions, use the s command with regex: sed 's/[0-9]+/number/' filename.txt This command replaces all sequences of digits with the word number.
To edit a file in place, use the -i option: sed -i 's/old/new/' filename.txt This command replaces old with new in the file filename.txt and saves the changes.
To execute multiple commands, use the -e option: sed -e 's/old/new/' -e '/pattern/d' filename.txt This command replaces old with new and deletes lines containing pattern.
To apply commands to specific lines or ranges of lines, use address ranges: sed '1,3s/old/new/' filename.txt This command replaces old with new in lines 1 to 3.
To combine sed with grep, use a pipeline: grep "pattern" filename.txt | sed 's/old/new/' This command first filters lines containing pattern and then replaces old with new.
To combine sed with awk, use a pipeline: awk '{print $1}' filename.txt | sed 's/old/new/' This command first prints the first field of each line and then replaces old with new.
To combine sed with find, use a pipeline: find /path/to/search -name "*.log" -exec sed -i 's/old/new/' {} \; This command finds all .log files and replaces old with new in each file.
To insert text before or after a pattern, use the i or a command: sed '/pattern/i\Insert this line before pattern' filename.txt sed '/pattern/a\Append this line after pattern' filename.txt

To append text to the end of a line, use the s command with a & to reference the matched pattern: sed 's/pattern/& append/' filename.txt This command appends append to the end of lines containing pattern.
To replace multiple patterns, use multiple s commands: sed 's/old1/new1/; s/old2/new2/' filename.txt This command replaces old1 with new1 and old2 with new2.

The sed command is a versatile and powerful tool for text processing and transformation. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use sed for a wide range of tasks, from simple text substitution to complex text manipulation and file editing.

sed Man Page GNU sed Documentation grep Man Page awk Man Page find Man Page By following these best practices, you can leverage the sed command to its full potential and efficiently manage your text processing and file editing tasks from the command line.

Monitoring and analyzing the status of a Kubernetes (K8s) cluster is crucial for maintaining the health and efficiency of your applications. The kubectl command-line tool provides powerful capabilities for interacting with and analyzing your Kubernetes cluster. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using kubectl to analyze cluster status, covering various scenarios such as checking cluster information, monitoring resources, troubleshooting issues, and performing advanced operations.
To get basic information about the cluster, use the kubectl cluster-info command: kubectl cluster-info This command displays the Kubernetes master and DNS endpoints.
To list all nodes in the cluster, use the kubectl get nodes command: kubectl get nodes This command displays the status, roles, age, and version of each node.
To list all namespaces in the cluster, use the kubectl get namespaces command: kubectl get namespaces This command displays the name and status of each namespace.
To list all pods in a namespace, use the kubectl get pods command: kubectl get pods -n <namespace> This command displays the name, ready status, status, restarts, and age of each pod.

To list all deployments in a namespace, use the kubectl get deployments command: kubectl get deployments -n <namespace> This command displays the name, desired replicas, current replicas, up-to-date replicas, and available replicas of each deployment.

To list all services in a namespace, use the kubectl get services command: kubectl get services -n <namespace> This command displays the name, type, cluster IP, external IP, and ports of each service.
To list all ConfigMaps in a namespace, use the kubectl get configmaps command: kubectl get configmaps -n <namespace> This command displays the name and age of each ConfigMap.
To list all Secrets in a namespace, use the kubectl get secrets command: kubectl get secrets -n <namespace> This command displays the name and age of each Secret.

To get detailed information about a specific resource, use the kubectl describe command: kubectl describe <resource> <name> -n <namespace> For example, to describe a pod: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> This command provides detailed information about the resource, including events and status.
To view the logs of a pod, use the kubectl logs command: kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace> To follow the logs in real-time, use the -f flag: kubectl logs -f <pod-name> -n <namespace>
To execute a command inside a running pod, use the kubectl exec command: kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- /bin/bash This command opens an interactive shell inside the pod.

To forward a local port to a port on a pod, use the kubectl port-forward command: kubectl port-forward <pod-name> <local-port>:<pod-port> -n <namespace> This command allows you to access the pod's service locally.
To check the status of a specific pod, use the kubectl get pods command: kubectl get pods <pod-name> -n <namespace> This command displays the status and other details of the pod.
To check the status of a specific node, use the kubectl get nodes command: kubectl get nodes <node-name> This command displays the status and other details of the node.
To check recent events in the cluster, use the kubectl get events command: kubectl get events -n <namespace> This command displays recent events, which can help diagnose issues.

To check resource limits and requests for a pod, use the kubectl describe command: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> This command provides detailed information about resource limits and requests.

To scale a deployment, use the kubectl scale command: kubectl scale deployment <deployment-name> --replicas=<number> -n <namespace> This command scales the deployment to the specified number of replicas.

To perform a rolling update on a deployment, use the kubectl rollout command: kubectl rollout restart deployment <deployment-name> -n <namespace> This command restarts the deployment, performing a rolling update.
To debug a pod, use the kubectl debug command: kubectl debug <pod-name> -n <namespace> This command creates a debugging container inside the pod.

Monitoring and analyzing the status of a Kubernetes cluster is essential for maintaining the health and efficiency of your applications. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use kubectl to interact with and analyze your Kubernetes cluster.

documents.s: Best Practices of tcpdump and netstat

documents.t: Network analysis is a critical skill for system administrators and network engineers. Tools like tcpdump, netstat, ping, traceroute, nmap, and iftop provide powerful capabilities for monitoring, diagnosing, and troubleshooting network issues. This article provides a comprehensive guide to the best practices of using these commands, covering various scenarios such as capturing and filtering network traffic, displaying network statistics, and diagnosing network issues.
To start capturing network traffic, use the following command: tcpdump This command captures all traffic on the default network interface.

To filter traffic by protocol, use the -i option: tcpdump -i eth0 To filter traffic by IP address, use the host keyword: tcpdump host 192.168.1.1 To filter traffic by port, use the port keyword: tcpdump port 80
To save captured traffic to a file, use the -w option: tcpdump -w capture.pcap
To read a saved capture file, use the -r option: tcpdump -r capture.pcap
To display all active connections, use the following command: netstat -a
To display active TCP connections, use the -t option: netstat -at
To display listening ports, use the -l option: netstat -lt
To display network statistics, use the -s option: netstat -s
To check connectivity to a host, use the ping command: ping google.com
To trace the route to a host, use the traceroute command: traceroute google.com
To scan for open ports on a host, use the nmap command: nmap 192.168.1.1
To monitor network traffic in real-time, use the iftop command: iftop -i eth0
To capture and analyze HTTP traffic, use tcpdump with port filtering: tcpdump -i eth0 port 80
To monitor real-time traffic on a specific interface, use iftop: iftop -i eth0
To diagnose network issues, use a combination of ping, traceroute, and tcpdump: ping google.com traceroute google.com tcpdump -i eth0 host google.com

Network analysis is a critical skill for maintaining and troubleshooting network infrastructure. By mastering the various options and scenarios covered in this article, you can effectively use tools like tcpdump, netstat, ping, traceroute, nmap, and iftop to monitor, diagnose, and troubleshoot network issues.

Introduction System Overview Session and Historical Message Management Communication Protocols and APIs Standardized Prompt Format Managing Historical Messages System Expansion Adding Cache Mechanism Scope of Caching Elastic Scalability Production Readiness Conclusion References

ChatGPT is a conversational system based on Large Language Models (LLMs). This article introduces the process of building a system similar to ChatGPT, covering everything from the model, inference engine, to the overall architecture.

Our primary focus will be on the core of the conversation system. System Diagram: +--------------+ | Web | | Interface | +--------------+ | | v +--------------+ | Server | +--------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Inference Runtime | | (LLM Inference Engine) | +--------------------------+ | | v +--------------+ | Response | +--------------+ In this basic system framework: The web interface interacts with users, The server receives user requests and forwards them to the inference runtime (inference engine), The inference runtime loads the LLM to generate a response, returning it to the user.

However, the above system has a critical flaw: it lacks session and historical message management for users. Common inference runtimes are typically stateless and do not directly support multi-turn conversations with historical context storage, meaning the system "forgets" previous exchanges within a single session. To address this, we need some essential modifications. Enhanced System Diagram: +--------------+ | Web | | Interface | +--------------+ | | v +--------------+ | Server | +--------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Inference Runtime | | (LLM Inference Engine) | +--------------------------+ | | v +--------------+ | Database | +--------------+ In this setup, we introduce a database component to store user sessions and historical messages.

For communication, the web interface and server can use HTTP protocols. Basic REST APIs might include: POST /chat: Initiate a new session. POST /chat/:chatID/completion: Continue a conversation within an existing session. GET /chats: Retrieve a list of sessions. DELETE /chat/:chatID: Delete a specific session. The server persists data in the database, structuring conversation messages with essential fields like userID, chatID, userMessage, and assistantMessage.

When sending data to the inference runtime, the server uses a standardized prompt format: [ { "role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant." }, { "role": "user", "content": "Hello!" }, { "role": "assistant", "content": "Hello there, how may I assist you today?" }, { "role": "user", "content": "How are you?" } ] The role field represents different participants: system defines the conversation context, user represents user input, and assistant represents the model’s output.

There are several ways to handle historical messages: Direct Prompt Filling: Add historical messages in the prompt as user and assistant entries. This works well for short conversations. Dynamic Context Adjustment: Discard earlier messages to fit within the LLM’s token limit. Message Summarization: Use the inference engine to summarize conversation history, compressing information before filling the prompt. With session and historical message management, we establish a basic system framework.
As the user base grows, the system will require further scalability.

One approach to scalability is implementing a cache to avoid repeated inference processes. The cache key-value pair would be the user's question and the AI's response. A cache hit would depend on whether the semantic content of the question is similar. For example, if two questions have different wording but the same meaning, the system should return the same response. Enhanced Caching System Diagram: +--------------+ | Web | | Interface | +--------------+ | | v +--------------+ | Server | +--------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Inference Runtime | | (LLM Inference Engine) | +--------------------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Embedding | | Runtime & Model | +--------------------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Vector Storage & Search | +--------------------------+ Apart from the cache module, we add embedding runtime and a text embedding model to convert text into vectors. If two vectors are close, their text content is semantically similar. Vector storage and search modules are used to store and retrieve vectors.

Caching can be scoped to: Single-user cache: Caching value is low as users rarely repeat the same question. Global cache: Allows reuse across users, but risks exposing sensitive data. After data analysis and validation, decide if cache implementation is beneficial.

Elastic scaling is another key to handling high concurrency. The server is stateless, which allows for easy horizontal scaling. Scalability System Diagram: +--------------+ | Web | | Interface | +--------------+ | | v +--------------+ | Gateway | | (Load Bal.) | +--------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Server Instances | +--------------------------+ | | v +--------------------------+ | Inference Runtimes | +--------------------------+ Here, we introduce a gateway for load balancing. The inference runtime is also stateless and supports elastic scaling, but it requires more hardware resources and may respond slower than the server. To maintain stability under peak load, add a message queue (MQ) and change request handling to asynchronous, improving system resilience.

The system architecture covers the basic logic, but to achieve production-readiness, further steps are necessary: Technology Selection: Choose a database (e.g., PostgreSQL or MongoDB) and inference engine (e.g., llama.cpp, HuggingFace Transformers, vLLM) and map logical components to physical components. Observability: Integrate logging, tracing, metrics, and set up monitoring and alerting. CI/CD and Deployment Environment: Configure automation pipelines for continuous integration and deployment, and select the appropriate environment (e.g., cloud platforms or Kubernetes).

A conversational AI system has several core components responsible for processing, generating, and managing dialogue flow with users. This overview explains the minimal structure for a functional, extensible ChatGPT-style system.
The architecture focuses on the interaction between the user, the web interface, and the inference engine that generates responses.

+---------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+ | Web UI | <-- HTTP --> | Server/API | <-- REST --> | Inference Runtime | | (User Access) | | (Request Routing) | | (LLM Model Handling) | +---------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+ ^ | |<--------------------------------------------------------+ Web UI: Handles user interaction and displays responses. Server/API: Receives requests and forwards them to the inference runtime. Inference Runtime: Loads the large language model (LLM), processes the input, and generates a response.

Standard inference runtimes are typically stateless, meaning they cannot recall previous messages in a conversation. To handle multi-turn dialogue, we integrate a database to persist session data and user message history.

+---------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+ | Web UI | <-- HTTP --> | Server/API | <-- REST --> | Inference Runtime | | | | | | | +---------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+ | +---------------- Database ----------------+ | User Session, ChatID, and Messages | +------------------------------------------+ Database: Stores user sessions, chat histories, and other metadata. Server/API: Uses REST endpoints to interact with the database, retrieving history when needed.
documents.s: Diagram: Enhanced System with Session and History Management

documents.t: The Server/API manages communication with the Web UI via REST APIs, handling user requests, responses, and session tracking. REST Endpoints: POST /chat: Starts a new conversation. POST /chat/:chatID/completion: Continues a conversation in an existing session. GET /chats: Retrieves the list of active sessions. DELETE /chat/:chatID: Deletes a specified session. Sample API Call to Start a Conversation curl -X POST http://yourserver.com/chat \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"userID": "12345", "message": "Hello, ChatGPT!"}'

The prompt format structures conversation history and provides context to the model. Example Prompt Format in JSON [ { "role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant." }, { "role": "user", "content": "Hello!" }, { "role": "assistant", "content": "Hello there, how may I assist you today?" }, { "role": "user", "content": "How are you?" } ] Role: Indicates the message source (system, user, or assistant). Content: The message text.

Direct Prompt Fill: Append all previous messages to the prompt, suitable for short interactions. Context Truncation: Omit older messages when context length exceeds the model’s token limit. History Summarization: Generate a summary of prior messages to condense the context, enabling longer conversations within token limits.
In a high-traffic environment, it is essential to scale the system horizontally and incorporate caching for repeated requests.
Implementing caching reduces redundant processing for similar queries. This approach involves caching semantic meanings of requests rather than exact matches.

+---------------+ +------------+ +----------------+ | User Query | -> Embedding -> | Cache | Cache Hit -> | Response | +---------------+ +------------+ +----------------+ | No Hit v +---------------------------+ +--------------------+ | Text Embedding Model | --> | Vector Storage and | | (e.g., BERT/Word2Vec) | | Search Database | +---------------------------+ +--------------------+ Embedding Runtime: Converts queries into vector embeddings. Vector Storage: Stores embeddings to detect semantically similar queries.
documents.s: Diagram: Cache with Vector Embeddings for Similar Query Detection

documents.t: Single User Cache: Stores responses per user session. Global Cache: Shared across all users, introducing potential privacy considerations.
Scaling is crucial for supporting high traffic. Stateless components like the server and inference runtime can be scaled horizontally using Kubernetes.

+--------------------------+ +---------------+ +--------------------------+ | Gateway | ---> | Server | ---> | Inference | | | | | | Runtime (Auto-scalable) | | Load Balancer | | (Stateless) | | | +--------------------------+ +---------------+ +--------------------------+ Gateway: Distributes traffic across multiple servers. Message Queue (MQ): Handles requests asynchronously for stable inference.
documents.s: Diagram: Load Balanced System Architecture with Elastic Scaling

documents.t: To make the system production-ready, additional steps are essential.

Technology Selection: Database: PostgreSQL or MongoDB for session persistence. Inference Engine: Use efficient models like llama.cpp, HuggingFace Transformers, or vLLM. Observability: Implement logging, tracing, and metrics. CI/CD and Deployment: Use Kubernetes or cloud-based deployment environments.

This guide provides a foundational approach to building a ChatGPT-like system, managing sessions, scaling the architecture, and ensuring production reliability. From basic dialogue to advanced caching and scalability, these steps can help create a highly responsive and robust conversational AI.
Prerequisites​ Node.js installed (version 14 or higher). npm or yarn for package management. A Google Cloud Platform (GCP) account to obtain the API Key and set up the Map ID.
documents.s: Building a Google Maps Application with React and TypeScript

documents.t: Node.js installed (version 14 or higher). npm or yarn for package management. A Google Cloud Platform (GCP) account to obtain the API Key and set up the Map ID.

Create a React Application: npx create-react-app google-maps-app --template typescript cd google-maps-app Install Required Dependencies: npm install @react-google-maps/api npm install react-hook-form Setup Google Cloud Platform: Enable the Maps JavaScript API: Go to the Google Cloud Console. Create a new project or select an existing one. Navigate to APIs & Services > Library and enable the Maps JavaScript API. Generate an API Key: Go to APIs & Services > Credentials and create an API Key. Restrict the API Key to ensure security by specifying HTTP referrers (your domain or localhost). Create a Map ID: Go to Google Maps Platform > Maps > Map Management. Create a new Map ID and configure it with desired styles and settings.
google-maps-app/ ├── public/ ├── src/ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── MapContainer.tsx │ │ ├── SearchBox.tsx │ ├── App.tsx │ ├── index.tsx │ ├── types/ │ │ ├── index.d.ts │ ├── utils/ │ ├── mapUtils.ts

Create src/types/index.d.ts to define types for the Google Maps objects: declare global { interface Window { google: any; } } export interface MarkerData { position: google.maps.LatLngLiteral; title: string; }

Create src/utils/mapUtils.ts to define helper functions: export const loadGoogleMapsScript = (apiKey: string): Promise<void> => { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const script = document.createElement('script'); script.src = `https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/js?key=${apiKey}&libraries=places`; script.async = true; script.defer = true; script.onload = () => resolve(); script.onerror = (e) => reject(e); document.head.appendChild(script); }); };

Create src/components/MapContainer.tsx: import React, { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'; import { MarkerData } from '../types'; type MapContainerProps = { apiKey: string; mapId: string; }; const MapContainer: React.FC<MapContainerProps> = ({ apiKey, mapId }) => { const mapRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null); const [map, setMap] = useState<google.maps.Map | null>(null); const [markers, setMarkers] = useState<google.maps.Marker[]>([]); useEffect(() => { const initMap = async () => { try { await loadGoogleMapsScript(apiKey); if (mapRef.current) { const mapInstance = new google.maps.Map(mapRef.current, { center: { lat: 37.7749, lng: -122.4194 }, zoom: 12, mapId: mapId, }); setMap(mapInstance); } } catch (error) { console.error('Failed to load Google Maps:', error); } }; initMap(); }, [apiKey, mapId]); const addMarker = (markerData: MarkerData) => { if (map) { const marker = new google.maps.marker.AdvancedMarkerElement({ map, position: markerData.position, title: markerData.title, }); setMarkers((prev) => [...prev, marker]); } }; return <div ref={mapRef} style={{ width: '100%', height: '500px' }} />; }; export default MapContainer;

Create src/components/SearchBox.tsx: import React, { useEffect, useRef } from 'react'; type SearchBoxProps = { onPlaceSelected: (place: google.maps.places.PlaceResult) => void; }; const SearchBox: React.FC<SearchBoxProps> = ({ onPlaceSelected }) => { const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null); useEffect(() => { if (inputRef.current) { const autocomplete = new google.maps.places.Autocomplete(inputRef.current); autocomplete.addListener('place_changed', () => { const place = autocomplete.getPlace(); if (place) { onPlaceSelected(place); } }); } }, []); return <input ref={inputRef} type="text" placeholder="Search places..." />; }; export default SearchBox;

Update src/App.tsx: import React, { useState } from 'react'; import MapContainer from './components/MapContainer'; import SearchBox from './components/SearchBox'; import { MarkerData } from './types'; const App: React.FC = () => { const [markers, setMarkers] = useState([]); const apiKey = 'YOUR_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY'; const mapId = 'YOUR_MAP_ID'; const handlePlaceSelected = (place: google.maps.places.PlaceResult) => { if (place.geometry?.location) { const markerData = { position: { lat: place.geometry.location.lat(), lng: place.geometry.location.lng(), }, title: place.name || '', }; setMarkers((prev) => [...prev, markerData]); } }; return (
); }; export default App;
Replace YOUR_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY and YOUR_MAP_ID in App.tsx with your actual values. Start the application: npm start Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser.

At 09:25 the call auction ends. At 09:30 the tape starts, and for the next four hours the Chinese market talks continuously — a central-bank operation, a futures point, an index level, a draft regulation, a company filing, an analyst note about the difference between two of them. All of it is real, and all of it is somewhere. But it is not in the same place. So you end up with six tabs open — a wire service, a quote page, a sector heatmap, a calendar, a filing index, a forum — and the tab bar quietly becomes the product. Every one of them is a different layout, a different colour scheme, a different idea of what matters, and most of them are built for somebody else's question. I kept wanting a single board. One page where the hot list, the 7×24 newsflash, sector heat, the economic calendar and the individual-stock hot list are all visible at once, and where every panel answers the same question: what changed, and how much does it matter? 财经今日 (CaiJing Today) is that board. It is Chinese-first, because that is the language the market speaks first, with English one click away.
documents.s: A market day is a lot of tabs

documents.t: This is the running site — caijing.today — with live data. On the left the TOP 50 hot ranking with its 1-hour / 24-hour / week / month windows and heat bars. In the middle the editorial picks, the market charts and the individual-stock hot list. On the right the 7×24 newsflash, the economic calendar and the global market quotes. The strip across the top scrolls the live quote tape. Open it and the shape is deliberately dense. A quote strip scrolls along the top. Below that, three columns of panels, each one a window onto the same database, none of them a summary of the others. Hot Ranking (热榜 / TOP 50) — headlines ranked by heat, with a window selector. The heat score is not editorial judgement; it is computed from publication time, the confidence of the analysis attached to the item, and how strong its sentiment is. Live Newsflash (7×24 快讯) — the newsflash. Short, timestamped, and it keeps its own rhythm while you read, so an article you opened five minutes ago still has the tape beside it. Hot Stocks (个股热榜) — the individual-stock hot list, with its own ranking. Categories (分类导航) — twelve categories: 宏观, 股市, 美股, 债券, 外汇, 大宗商品, 加密, 房产, 科技, 公司, 政策, 观点. They are not a hand-made taxonomy — each item is classified from its signal type, sectors, region and tags, and you can disagree with the result by hand. Economic Calendar (经济日历) — the day's scheduled releases, with an importance rating. Market Data / Trending / Global Markets (数据图表 / 热搜关键词 / 全球市场) — the index sparklines, the trending keywords, and the global quote board. Sector Heat / Crypto Market (行业板块 / 加密市场) — the sector heatmap with capital inflow, and the crypto board with coins, chains and TVL. And the whole thing is in two languages, with the toggle in the header. The Chinese is not a translation of the English — the Chinese is the original layout, and English was added beside it. The same board in the light theme. The board is dark by default; the toggle in the header switches it, and the choice is remembered.

Frontend — React 19, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Query, i18next. Strict types, and 55 tests. Backend — FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2 over asyncpg, Pydantic. Read-only: the service never writes to the database it reads. Database — PostgreSQL 17. Fifteen tables and two views, published as docs/SCHEMA.sql. API — seventeen endpoints under /api/v1, all of them reads. Licence — MIT, for the whole repository. Tests — 25 backend, 55 frontend, and four CI gates: the backend suite, a schema job that applies the contract to a real PostgreSQL and checks the ORM mirror against it, the frontend suite, and a Docker build of all four images. This post is not the documentation. The documentation is the repository: the schema contract, the setup guide, the data-source rules and the test matrix. I would rather you read those than take my word for it. 👉 github.com/whereq/CaiJing-Today To run it: git clone https://github.com/whereq/CaiJing-Today.git cd CaiJing-Today cp docker/.env.example docker/.env docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d --build Then open http://localhost:8080. That is the whole stack — PostgreSQL 17, the schema contract, the demo data, the API and the frontend. The API is on http://localhost:8000, with interactive documentation at /docs. You do not need any keys to build, test or run it. The defaults in docker/.env.example are local development credentials, not secrets, and the site works with no identity provider at all: browsing is public, so the UI stays in anonymous mode and the sign-in control is hidden.

Because the collector is the part that is not open, and the schema is the part that is. This repository ships the schema as an explicit contract — 15 tables, two views, the column types, the unique constraints, the snapshot discipline, the UTC rules — and a FastAPI service that reads it and nothing else. The collector that fills those tables in production is a separate component. I think that split is the useful bit. The schema is not a dump of somebody else's database; it is the agreement between two programs that are allowed to be written by different people. If you want your own collector — your own sources, your own cadence, your own idea of what a headline is — you write a component that inserts into those tables, and the API and the interface serve it with no code changes. That is the whole extension point, and it is documented in docs/data-sources.md: what published_at means, why the snapshot tables take a new as_of instead of an update, which category ids are legal, and what the heat score is made of. One warning, because it matters. The MIT licence covers the code. It says nothing about the data you put into the database. The headlines, quotes and filings a collector retrieves belong to the organisations that published them, each under its own terms, and a financial wire, a free public-data portal and a market-data vendor do not grant the same rights. If you connect real data, complying with those terms is your job, not this project's. And to be plain about the demo dataset: every row in it is invented. The headlines are prefixed 【示例】 / [sample], the prices are fabricated, the calendar entries are placeholders, the links use the reserved .invalid TLD, and the hot-stock list uses DEMO-001 … DEMO-010 rather than real tickers. That is deliberate. A real ticker next to a fabricated heat score reads as investment advice. This is what a fresh checkout gives you: the same board, running on the synthetic demo dataset. Every headline is marked 【示例】, every ticker reads DEMO-001 … DEMO-010, and nothing in it is real. The interface is Chinese-first, as it is on the live site.
documents.s: Why it is in the world now

documents.t: This app stands on the work of other people, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Polygon.io — market data. The quote strip, the index levels, the charts. GDELT — the global news index behind the gdelt source id. SEC EDGAR — the US filing index behind the sec_edgar source id. 东方财富 (Eastmoney) — the 全球快讯 and 财经早餐 feeds the interface credits as akshare_em_global and akshare_em_cjzc. 财经 RSS 聚合 — the finance RSS feeds behind the rss source id. React, Vite, TanStack Query, i18next, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, PostgreSQL, nginx and Docker — the stack this repository is built on. The dependency list is in NOTICE. The demo dataset is also the work of nobody in particular, which is exactly the point: it is synthetic, it says so, and it exists so that a fresh checkout has something to show. If you write a collector against the schema — or fork the board for a market this one does not cover — I would genuinely like to hear about it.

九点二十五，集合竞价结束。九点半，开盘。从这一刻起，接下来四个小时， 市场一直在说话：一次公开市场操作、一个期货点位、一个指数点位、一份征求意见 稿、一份公司公告，再加上一篇分析——而这两者到底差在哪。 这些消息都是真的，也都真实存在。只是它们不在同一个地方。 于是你打开六个标签页：行情快讯、指数页面、板块热力图、日历、公告检索、还有 一个论坛。它们各自的版式、配色、关注点都不一样，而且大多是为别人的问题而 做的。 我一直想要的是一块板子。一屏之内，热榜、7×24 快讯、板块热力、经济日历、个股 热榜同时都在；而且每个面板回答的都是同一个问题：发生了什么变化，有多重要。 财经今日（CaiJing Today） 就是这块板子。它以中文为默认界面，因为市场先说 中文；英文放在旁边，一键可切。
documents.s: 一个交易日，是六个标签页

documents.t: 这是运行中的站点——caijing.today——里面是真实数据。左侧是热榜 TOP 50，配 1 小时 / 24 小时 / 本周 / 本月四档时间窗和热度条；中间是编辑精选、 行情图表和个股热榜；右侧是 7×24 快讯、经济日历和全球市场行情；顶部那条是滚动的 行情带。 打开它，版式是刻意做密的。顶部一条行情带横向滚动。往下是三栏面板，每一个都是 同一套数据库的一个切面，谁也不替谁做总结。 热榜 / TOP 50 —— 按热度排序的新闻，右侧可切换时间窗。这里的热度不是编辑 判断，而是由发布时间、该条所挂分析的可信度，以及情绪强度共同算出来的。 7×24 快讯 —— 快讯流。短、带时间戳，有自己的节奏；你读一篇五分钟前打开 的稿子，它也还在旁边走着。 个股热榜 —— 个股热榜，自带一套排序。 分类导航 —— 十二个分类：宏观、股市、美股、债券、外汇、大宗商品、加密、 房产、科技、公司、政策、观点。这不是手工维护的分类表——每一条内容是按它的 信号类型、板块、地域和标签归类的，你也可以手动改。 经济日历 —— 当天的预定数据发布，带重要度。 数据图表 / 行业板块 / 加密市场 / 热搜关键词 —— 走势图、带资金流的板块 热力、加密板块，以及大家正在搜什么。 整套界面两种语言，切换按钮在页头。中文不是英文的翻译——中文才是最初的版式， 英文是后来并排加上去的。 同一块板子的浅色主题。板子默认是深色的，页头的切换按钮可以换，切换结果会 被记住。

前端 —— React 19、TypeScript、Vite、TanStack Query、i18next。类型严格， 55 个测试。 后端 —— FastAPI、SQLAlchemy 2（asyncpg 异步驱动）、Pydantic。 只读：这个服务从不写入它所读的数据库。 数据库 —— PostgreSQL 17。15 张表、2 个视图，以 docs/SCHEMA.sql 的形式公开。 API —— /api/v1 下 17 个接口，全部是读。 许可 —— MIT，覆盖整个仓库。 测试 —— 后端 25 个、前端 55 个，CI 里四道关：后端测试、一道把库表契约 真正灌进 PostgreSQL 并和 ORM 映射对账的 schema 检查、前端测试，以及四个镜像 的 Docker 构建。 这篇文章不是文档。 文档是仓库本身：库表契约、安装指南、数据来源的规矩、 测试矩阵。我更希望你直接去读那些，而不是听我一面之词。 👉 github.com/whereq/CaiJing-Today 跑起来： git clone https://github.com/whereq/CaiJing-Today.git cd CaiJing-Today cp docker/.env.example docker/.env docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d --build 然后打开 http://localhost:8080。这就是完整的一栈——PostgreSQL 17、库表契约、 演示数据、API 和前端。API 在 http://localhost:8000，交互式文档在 /docs。 构建、测试、运行都不需要任何 key。 docker/.env.example 里的默认值是本地 开发用的凭据，不是密钥；而且不需要身份提供者：浏览是公开的，所以界面停在匿名 模式，登录入口自动隐藏。

因为采集器是那部分不开源的，而库表结构是开源的。 这个仓库把库表结构当作一份明确的契约公开——15 张表、2 个视图，列的类型、唯一 约束、快照的纪律、时间的 UTC 规矩——再加上一个只读它的 FastAPI 服务。生产环境 里往这些表里灌数据的采集器是另一个组件。 我觉得这个切分才是有用的地方。库表结构不是谁家数据库的导出物，它是两个允许 由不同的人写的程序之间的约定。如果你想要自己的采集器——自己的信源、自己的节 奏、自己对「一条新闻」的理解——那就写一个往这些表里插入的组件，API 和界面不 改一行代码就会把它伺服出来。 这就是全部的扩展点，规矩写在 docs/data-sources.md里： published_at 是什么时区、为什么快照表要新增一个 as_of 而不是更新、哪些分 类 id 是合法的、热度分数由什么构成。 有一句必须说清楚的话。 MIT 许可覆盖的是代码，它对往数据库里放的数据只 字未提。采集器取回来的标题、行情和公告，权利属于发布它们的那家机构，各有各的 条款；财经通讯社、免费公开数据门户和行情数据商给的授权根本不是一回事。你要是 接了真实数据，守约是你的事，不是这个项目的。 还有关于演示数据，说白了：里面每一行都是编的。标题带【示例】/ [sample] 前缀， 价格是假的，日历条目是占位的，链接用的是保留域名 .invalid，热榜里的代码是 DEMO-001 … DEMO-010 而不是真实股票代码。这是有意的——真实代码配一个编出来 的热度，读起来就成了投资建议。 这就是一份全新 checkout 跑起来的样子：同一块板子，跑在合成演示数据上。每条 标题都标着【示例】，代码全是 DEMO-001 … DEMO-010，里面没有一个数字是真的。 界面和线上一样，默认中文。

Cluster Node Pod Deployment Service Ingress ConfigMap Secret Persistent Volume (PV) and Persistent Volume Claim (PVC) Namespace DaemonSet Job and CronJob Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) StatefulSet Volume and StorageClass NetworkPolicy Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) Helm Charts This guide provides a detailed overview of Kubernetes concepts, examples, use cases, installation YAML examples, and visual representations of the architecture.

A Kubernetes Cluster is a group of nodes (machines) that host and manage containerized applications. Each cluster has at least one master node, which controls the state of the cluster, and multiple worker nodes.
A cloud-based cluster with one master node and multiple worker nodes in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

An ideal setup for running a production microservices application with high availability. YAML Structure for Cluster Creation​ apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 kind: Cluster nodes: - role: control-plane - role: worker - role: worker - role: worker
A Node is a single machine within a Kubernetes cluster, capable of running one or more pods.
In a cloud environment, each node could be a virtual machine instance.

Nodes distribute workloads across the infrastructure. YAML Snippet​ The node configuration is usually specified by the cluster management tool (e.g., GKE or EKS) rather than in YAML, as it pertains to the infrastructure layer.
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, which can contain one or more containers.
A pod running a web server container and a logging container.

Running tightly coupled applications together within the same lifecycle. YAML Structure for Pod​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: web-server-pod spec: containers: - name: web-server image: nginx - name: logger image: fluentd
A Deployment is a Kubernetes object for managing a group of identical pods. It provides capabilities like rolling updates and rollback.
A deployment with three replicas of a web server pod.

Maintaining a stable version of an application by managing pod replicas. YAML Structure for Deployment​ apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: web-deployment spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: web template: metadata: labels: app: web spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.17.4
A Service provides a stable endpoint for accessing a set of pods.
A service that exposes an application to the public internet.

Load balancing traffic to an application across multiple pods. YAML Structure for Service​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: web-service spec: type: LoadBalancer selector: app: web ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 80
Ingress manages external access to services, typically using HTTP.
An ingress with rules to route traffic to different services based on URL paths.

Routing /api to backend services and /static to frontend services on the same domain. YAML Structure for Ingress​ apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: example-ingress spec: rules: - host: example.com http: paths: - path: /api pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: api-service port: number: 80 - path: /static pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: static-service port: number: 80
A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration data.
A ConfigMap for environment-specific variables.

Keeping configuration separate from the application code. YAML Structure for ConfigMap​ apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: config-demo data: DATABASE_URL: "jdbc:mysql://dbhost:3306/mydatabase" DEBUG_LEVEL: "3"
A Secret stores sensitive information, like passwords and tokens.
A secret containing API keys for external services.
Securing sensitive data without exposing it in the code. YAML Structure for Secret​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: api-key-secret type: Opaque data: api-key: c29tZS1yYW5kb20ta2V5Cg==
A Persistent Volume provides storage, while a Persistent Volume Claim is a request for that storage.

Ensuring data persistence for applications that require durable storage. YAML Structure for PV and PVC​ apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata: name: pv-storage spec: capacity: storage: 10Gi accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce hostPath: path: "/mnt/data" --- apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: pvc-storage spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce resources: requests: storage: 8Gi
A Namespace is a way to divide cluster resources among multiple users.
Separate namespaces for development, staging, and production environments.
Organizing resources for different environments or teams. YAML Structure for Namespace​ apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: dev-environment
A DaemonSet ensures that specific pods run on each node.
Running a logging agent on every node in the cluster.

Managing node-wide services like logging or monitoring. YAML Structure for DaemonSet​ apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: DaemonSet metadata: name: logger spec: selector: matchLabels: name: logger template: metadata: labels: name: logger spec: containers: - name: fluentd image: fluent/fluentd
Job runs a one-time task, while CronJob schedules a recurring task.
A Job to back up a database once and a CronJob to clean up logs daily.

Automating scheduled tasks or batch processing. YAML Structure for Job and CronJob​ apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata: name: backup-job spec: template: spec: containers: - name: backup image: backup-tool restartPolicy: OnFailure --- apiVersion: batch/v1beta1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: daily-cleanup spec: schedule: "0 0 * * *" jobTemplate: spec: template: spec: containers: - name: cleanup image: cleanup-tool restartPolicy: OnFailure
The HPA scales pod replicas automatically based on resource utilization.
Scaling web server pods based on CPU usage.

Scaling applications to handle variable workloads. YAML Structure for HPA​ apiVersion: autoscaling/v1 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: name: web-hpa spec: scaleTarget Ref: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment name: web-deployment minReplicas: 1 maxReplicas: 10 targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 70

A StatefulSet for a MongoDB replica set.

Managing stateful applications where each instance requires its own storage. YAML Structure for StatefulSet​ apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: StatefulSet metadata: name: mongo spec: serviceName: "mongo" replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: mongo template: metadata: labels: app: mongo spec: containers: - name: mongo image: mongo ports: - containerPort: 27017 name: mongo

SSD-based storage for a database application.

Choosing storage for applications based on performance requirements. NetworkPolicy defines network access rules between pods.
Restricting access to specific pods.

Securing inter-service communication. YAML Structure for NetworkPolicy​ apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: deny-all spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress ingress: [] egress: []
CRDs extend Kubernetes by allowing users to create custom resources.
A custom resource to manage database schema migrations.

Adding domain-specific resources for applications. YAML Structure for CRD​ apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind: CustomResourceDefinition metadata: name: migrations.mycompany.com spec: group: mycompany.com versions: - name: v1 served: true storage: true scope: Namespaced names: plural: migrations singular: migration kind: Migration
Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes, and Helm Charts are pre-configured packages.
A Helm chart for deploying a WordPress site.

Simplifying application deployment and management. Example Helm Command​ helm install my-wordpress bitnami/wordpress These concepts are essential for understanding and operating Kubernetes in production, allowing you to deploy, manage, and scale applications effectively. Each example and YAML configuration highlights the power and flexibility Kubernetes offers in a variety of scenarios.
