documents.t: /** * Mono represents a stream that emits 0 or 1 element * Perfect for: HTTP responses, database saves, single calculations */ public class MonoDeepDive { // Creation examples public void monoCreation() { // Empty Mono Mono<String> empty = Mono.empty(); // From value Mono<String> staticValue = Mono.just("Hello World"); // From nullable String possiblyNull = getFromCache(); Mono<String> nullable = Mono.justOrEmpty(possiblyNull); // From supplier (lazy) Mono<String> lazy = Mono.fromSupplier(() -> expensiveOperation()); // From callable Mono<String> fromCallable = Mono.fromCallable(() -> { return database.getUser(userId); // Potentially blocking }); // From future CompletableFuture<String> future = asyncHttpCall(); Mono<String> fromFuture = Mono.fromFuture(future); } // Real-world use case: User profile lookup public Mono<UserProfile> getUserProfile(String userId) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> userRepository.findById(userId)) .filter(Optional::isPresent) .map(Optional::get) .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new UserNotFoundException(userId))); } }

/** * Flux represents a stream that emits 0 to N elements * Perfect for: Collections, real-time streams, paginated results */ public class FluxDeepDive { // Creation examples public void fluxCreation() { // From values Flux<String> fromValues = Flux.just("A", "B", "C"); // From array Flux<String> fromArray = Flux.fromArray(new String[]{"A", "B", "C"}); // From iterable Flux<String> fromList = Flux.fromIterable(Arrays.asList("A", "B", "C")); // Range Flux<Integer> numbers = Flux.range(1, 10); // Interval (real-time stream) Flux<Long> ticker = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // Generate (stateful stream) Flux<Integer> fibonacci = Flux.generate( () -> new int[]{0, 1}, // initial state (state, sink) -> { sink.next(state[0]); int next = state[0] + state[1]; state[0] = state[1]; state[1] = next; return state; } ); } // Real-world use case: Real-time stock prices public Flux<StockPrice> getStockPrices(String symbol) { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .flatMap(tick -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> stockService.getCurrentPrice(symbol)) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) ) .take(100); // Only take 100 price updates } }

public class TransformationOperators { /** * map: Synchronous 1:1 transformation * Use when: Transformation is fast, non-blocking, CPU-bound */ public void mapOperator() { Flux<String> names = Flux.just("john", "jane", "bob"); // Synchronous transformation - stays in same thread Flux<String> capitalized = names.map(name -> name.toUpperCase()); // Output: JOHN, JANE, BOB // Real-world: Data enrichment (fast) Flux<User> users = getUserIds() .map(id -> new User(id, "user-" + id)); } /** * flatMap: Asynchronous 1:N transformation * Use when: Need to call async APIs, database, external services */ public void flatMapOperator() { Flux<String> userIds = Flux.just("user1", "user2", "user3"); // Asynchronous transformation - can change threads Flux<User> users = userIds.flatMap(id -> userRepository.findByIdAsync(id) // Returns Mono<User> ); // Real-world: Fetch user details from multiple services Flux<Order> orders = getOrderIds() .flatMap(orderId -> orderService.getOrderAsync(orderId) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()) // Skip failed orders ); } /** * flatMapMany: Convert Mono to Flux * Use when: You have Mono that emits multiple items */ public void flatMapManyOperator() { Mono<String> csvData = readCsvFile(); // Convert Mono<String> to Flux<String[]> Flux<String[]> rows = csvData.flatMapMany(content -> Flux.fromArray(content.split("\n")) .map(line -> line.split(",")) ); // Real-world: Get user and their recent activities Mono<User> user = getUserProfile(userId); Flux<Activity> activities = user.flatMapMany(u -> activityService.getRecentActivities(u.getId()) ); } }

documents.t: public class AdvancedTransformations { /** * concatMap vs flatMap - Ordering guarantee */ public void orderingGuarantees() { Flux<String> ids = Flux.just("1", "2", "3"); // flatMap - no ordering guarantee (faster) Flux<String> unordered = ids.flatMap(id -> asyncOperation(id).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(randomDelay())) ); // concatMap - preserves order (slower but ordered) Flux<String> ordered = ids.concatMap(id -> asyncOperation(id).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(randomDelay())) ); // Real-world: Processing messages with ordering requirement Flux<Message> kafkaMessages = kafkaReceiver.receive(); kafkaMessages .concatMap(msg -> processMessage(msg)) // Maintain message order .subscribe(); } /** * switchMap - Cancel previous emissions */ public void switchMapOperator() { // Real-world: Search-as-you-type Flux<String> searchTerms = keyPressEvents(); Flux<SearchResults> results = searchTerms .debounce(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // Wait for typing to stop .switchMap(term -> searchService.search(term) // Cancel previous search if new term arrives .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) ); } /** * groupBy - Group elements by key */ public void groupByOperator() { // Real-world: Group orders by customer Flux<Order> orders = orderStream(); Flux<GroupedFlux<String, Order>> byCustomer = orders .groupBy(Order::getCustomerId); // Process each customer's orders separately byCustomer.flatMap(group -> group .window(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // Window by time .flatMap(window -> calculateCustomerStats(window)) ).subscribe(); } }

public class CombinationOperators { /** * zip - Combine multiple publishers */ public void zipOperator() { Mono<User> user = getUser(userId); Mono<Profile> profile = getProfile(userId); Mono<Preferences> prefs = getPreferences(userId); // Wait for all to complete, then combine Mono<UserDashboard> dashboard = Mono.zip(user, profile, prefs) .map(tuple -> { User u = tuple.getT1(); Profile p = tuple.getT2(); Preferences pref = tuple.getT3(); return new UserDashboard(u, p, pref); }); // Real-world: Aggregate data from multiple microservices Mono<OrderDetails> orderDetails = Mono.zip( orderService.getOrder(orderId), paymentService.getPayment(orderId), shippingService.getTracking(orderId) ).map(t -> OrderDetails.aggregate(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); } /** * merge vs concat - Parallel vs sequential combination */ public void mergeVsConcat() { Flux<String> stream1 = Flux.just("A", "B", "C").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)); Flux<String> stream2 = Flux.just("1", "2", "3").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(50)); // merge - interleaves as they arrive (faster) Flux<String> merged = Flux.merge(stream1, stream2); // Possible output: 1, A, 2, B, 3, C // concat - waits for first to complete (ordered) Flux<String> concatenated = Flux.concat(stream1, stream2); // Guaranteed output: A, B, C, 1, 2, 3 } /** * combineLatest - Combine latest from multiple streams */ public void combineLatest() { // Real-world: Real-time dashboard with multiple data sources Flux<Double> stockPrice = stockPriceStream(); Flux<Double> exchangeRate = exchangeRateStream(); Flux<News> newsFeed = newsStream(); Flux<Dashboard> dashboard = Flux.combineLatest( Arrays::asList, stockPrice, exchangeRate, newsFeed ).map(data -> { Double price = (Double) data[0]; Double rate = (Double) data[1]; News news = (News) data[2]; return new Dashboard(price, rate, news); }); } }

public class ErrorHandlingOperators { /** * Comprehensive error handling strategies */ public void errorHandling() { Flux<String> dataStream = getDataStream(); dataStream // 1. Timeout handling .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // 2. Retry with backoff .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 3. Fallback values .onErrorReturn("fallback-value") // 4. Fallback method .onErrorResume(error -> { if (error instanceof TimeoutException) { return getCachedData(); } else if (error instanceof DatabaseException) { return getBackupData(); } return Flux.error(error); }) // 5. Log and continue .doOnError(error -> log.error("Stream processing failed", error) ) .subscribe(); } /** * Circuit breaker pattern */ public void circuitBreaker() { CircuitBreaker circuitBreaker = CircuitBreaker.ofDefaults("backendService"); Flux<String> resilientStream = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .flatMap(tick -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> externalService.call()) .transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(circuitBreaker)) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just("fallback")) ); } }

public class SchedulingDeepDive { /** * Proper threading model for different operations */ public void schedulingOperators() { // CPU-intensive work Flux<Integer> cpuIntensive = Flux.range(1, 1000) .parallel() // Process in parallel .runOn(Schedulers.parallel()) .map(i -> expensiveComputation(i)) .sequential(); // I/O intensive work Flux<String> ioIntensive = Flux.just("id1", "id2", "id3") .flatMap(id -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> database.query(id)) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // Offload blocking I/O ); // Real-time processing with different schedulers Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(10)) .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) // Dedicated thread for downstream .map(tick -> transformData(tick)) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // Switch threads for I/O .flatMap(data -> saveToDatabase(data)) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.parallel()) // Where subscription happens .subscribe(); } /** * Scheduler types and when to use them */ public void schedulerTypes() { // Schedulers.immediate() - Current thread // Schedulers.single() - Single dedicated thread // Schedulers.parallel() - Fixed pool for CPU work // Schedulers.boundedElastic() - For blocking I/O (preferred over elastic) // Schedulers.elastic() - Legacy, unlimited threads (avoid) } }

public class ApiGatewayService { public Flux<ApiResponse> handleConcurrentRequests(Flux<ApiRequest> requests) { return requests .window(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // Window by time .flatMap(window -> window .limitRate(100) // Limit to 100 requests per second .flatMap(this::processRequest, 10) // Max 10 concurrent ) .onErrorResume(error -> Flux.just(ApiResponse.error("Service unavailable")) ); } private Mono<ApiResponse> processRequest(ApiRequest request) { return Mono.zip( userService.validateToken(request.getToken()), rateLimitService.checkLimit(request.getUserId()) ) .flatMap(tuple -> routingService.routeRequest(request)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) .retryWhen(Retry.fixedDelay(2, Duration.ofMillis(100))); } }

documents.t: public class DataPipeline { public Flux<ProcessedData> createPipeline() { return kafkaSource.stream() .groupBy(message -> message.getPartitionKey()) // Maintain ordering per key .flatMap(partitionStream -> partitionStream .window(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) // Batch processing .flatMap(this::processBatch) .flatMap(this::enrichWithExternalData) .flatMap(this::validateAndTransform) .buffer(100) // Buffer for bulk insert .flatMap(this::bulkInsertToDatabase) , 32) // Process 32 partitions concurrently .metrics() // Monitor performance .doOnNext(metrics::recordProcessingTime); } private Mono<ProcessedData> processBatch(Flux<Message> batch) { return batch .collectList() .flatMap(list -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> sparkService.processBatch(list)) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) ); } }

public class ResilientServiceComposition { public Mono<OrderResult> processOrder(Order order) { return validateOrder(order) .flatMap(validated -> Mono.zip( reserveInventory(validated).onErrorReturn(InventoryReservation.failed()), processPayment(validated).onErrorReturn(PaymentResult.failed()), updateShipping(validated).onErrorReturn(ShippingUpdate.failed()) ) ) .map(tuple -> { // Compose final result from partial successes/failures return OrderResult.fromComponents( tuple.getT1(), tuple.getT2(), tuple.getT3() ); }) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofSeconds(1))); } }

public class PerformanceBestPractices { // 1. Avoid blocking in reactive chains public Flux<String> badExample() { return Flux.range(1, 100) .map(i -> { return blockingDatabaseCall(i); // ❌ BLOCKING! }); } public Flux<String> goodExample() { return Flux.range(1, 100) .flatMap(i -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> blockingDatabaseCall(i)) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // ✅ Correct ); } // 2. Use backpressure properly public Flux<Data> handleBackpressure() { return fastProducer() .onBackpressureBuffer(1000) // Buffer up to 1000 elements .onBackpressureDrop(dropped -> log.warn("Dropped: {}", dropped)) .concatMap(this::slowConsumer, 5); // Control concurrency } // 3. Monitor and tune public void monitoring() { Flux.range(1, 1000) .name("processing.pipeline") .tag("type", "batch") .metrics() .doOnNext(item -> Metrics.counter("items.processed").increment() ) .subscribe(); } }

A component library is easy to publish and easy to ignore. The README shows a picture of a button. The demo page shows a page somebody built to look like the library, with the real component never loaded. The actual code sits in somebody's app, behind a build step, where you cannot see it — so the one thing you want to check, does this thing work when it is really installed?, is the one thing nobody checks. That is the gap this page closes. whereq.ca now has a live demo of @whereq/react — and a playground to try it in. The WhereQ Lab is built from one shared React component library. It lives on npm as @whereq/react, and the Lab now runs it in full: open /react and the real components from the published package render in front of you — not a screenshot of one, and not a story about one. If the demo breaks, the package is broken. That is the whole point of it.
documents.s: A library you cannot trust from a README

documents.t: The registry keyed it under "uk" while the demo asked for "gb", so the chip came back empty. "gb" is the key now, "uk" stays as an alias, and an unknown country draws a neutral emblem instead of an empty box. That one is worth writing down, because it is the kind of defect this page exists to catch: the flag was not broken in the demo, it was broken in the package, and it had been broken in the package the whole time. Nothing about a screenshot would ever have shown it.

documents.t: This one rests on a few other people's work, and it should say so. @whereq/react is MIT-licensed and © WhereQ. The Toast, Tag, Avatar, SearchBox and CountryFlag primitives were written for the WhereQ apps and then given away. The picture in the middle of my phone is 4:3, with black bars on either side — and those bars are not wasted, they hold the keyboard. The picture is a blue DOS banner and a prompt: C:\> The cursor blinks. It does not explain itself, and it does not need to. This is a 1994 machine — a 486, a sound card, a two-button mouse — and it fits in one hand. Everything I used to type into it still works: cd, dir, copy, mount c .. It works because it is the same machine: DOSBox r4305 running as a native library inside the APK, not in a browser tab, not in a WebView. Native code, in your pocket, at native speed.
documents.s: WhereQ-DOSBox: a DOS machine in your pocket

documents.t: FIFA 96 in the middle, the two console pads in the letterbox bars either side, and the 1990 World Cup song under it — all of it the real DOSBox core, running natively inside the APK.

WhereQ-DOSBox is a native Android port of DOSBox. The core is DOSBox r4305 from the SDL2 branch, imported from Em-DOSBox — Boris Gjenero's Emscripten build — and compiled for Android with the NDK and CMake into libdosbox.so, which ships inside the APK. The welcome screen and the C:> prompt. Touch moves the DOS mouse; the keys type into DOSBox. It runs on arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x86_64 — three ABIs in one APK — and needs Android 5.0 or newer. The licence is GPL-2.0, because the core is GPLv2 and that licence leaves no choice. The app collects nothing and never asks for the INTERNET permission, so it cannot send anything anywhere.

The File button opens the launcher. A bundle is a .zip of DOS software — a game, a utility, a text-mode program; it is called a bundle because it need not be a game. Three ways in: Install a bundle (.zip) through the system file picker, install all bundles from a folder, or Open with WhereQ-DOSBox from a file manager. None of them asks for a storage permission: the picker hands out the access, and the app only sees what you picked. A bundle unpacks into C:\GAMES\<n> with a generated RUN.BAT; Start file… picks the entry point by hand when the guess is wrong. Files are stored under their DOS 8.3 names — upper case, eight characters plus three. That is not decoration: DOSBox caches the drive listing, so a file whose name DOS can spell is still found after the emulator started, and a program asking for RESOURCE.CFG ends up at RESOURC.CFG, as on a real DOS. The launcher. Two ways in, and the licence and the privacy policy in the footer.

The DOS picture is 4:3 and centred, so in landscape the keys live in the black bars beside it, one hand on each side, the way a handheld console is built. The left pad holds the arrow keys as a D-pad, the left half of a split QWERTY, and File, Esc, Tab, RMB along the top. The right pad holds Alt, Ctrl, Shift, Space, Enter, the right half of the QWERTY, and #+=, Fn, Backspace. Nothing covers the picture. One hand on each side — and the #+= layer is on here, so the punctuation sits where the letters were. The letter layer already carries : . / \, so a DOS path needs no layer switch. #+= swaps both halves for the punctuation, Fn for F1–F12 and the other function keys. Ctrl, Alt and Shift work both ways: tap one and it stays armed for the next key, hold it and it behaves like a real key while the other thumb steers. The layout follows the screen: a letterbox bar of at least 116 dp gets the full pads, a narrower one a single column per side and the fold-up QWERTY, portrait a slim strip along the bottom. The letter keys come to about 33 dp wide on a 20:9 screen and 24 dp on an 18:9 one. Below 116 dp the pads become one column of keys per side. The keyboard icon in the left column folds the whole QWERTY up from the bottom. The QWERTY folded up out of the way, over the picture. The same key puts it away again.

A DOS mouse has two buttons and a touchscreen has one. The first finger holds the left button as long as it is down, so a drag drags. RMB sends a right click where the cursor stands, and a second finger does the same at its own position. Both are held, not tapped: a game that reads the mouse live — the button state at INT 33h AX=3 — misses an instantaneous click.

With the pads showing, switch Caps Lock on (double-tap Shift) and type the code everybody already has in their fingers: ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A The pads flip into a gamepad: an eight-way D-pad, a trackball, and Y, X, CTRL, ALT, SPACE and ENT. The code is matched on the case of the letters, so a lowercase ba just types ba into the DOS prompt. Game Mode. The letter pads are gone; a D-pad and a trackball take their place, in the same two bars. Game Mode, with the remap screen open. The gold outline marks the buttons that can be remapped. Long-press the gold profile button and pick Remap buttons…; the remap belongs to that one game and is remembered. The D-pad output cycles between ARROWS, NUMPAD and WASD, and the button carries the name of the mode you actually have. The same code on the D-pad (then X, Y) takes you back, and the Back button does it too. The gamepad sends the same SDL events the keyboard sends, so the guest cannot tell the two apart — no new input path for a 1994 game to learn.
documents.s: Game Mode: the pads turn into a gamepad

documents.t: Every game gets three slots. Save freezes the running machine — the CPU, the DOS memory, the video memory, the open DOS file handles, the hardware timers — and Load jumps back to that exact moment. A slot is a file on the phone, so it survives quitting the app and rebooting the phone. The sound chips are part of the machine too. The FM chip is snapshotted exactly — envelope, wave phase, LFO counter — so a note continues from the middle of its attack instead of starting over, and the PC speaker comes back silent. Resume restores the newest save state of the last game and names it: Resume STARFALL · slot 1 · 5 min ago.

A slot lives in the app's own storage, and Android deletes that when the app is uninstalled. Pick a folder on the phone — Config → Saves folder, or the offer after the first save — and every slot is mirrored there, gzipped, next to the game itself. A reinstall, a new phone, an app deleted by accident: they all come back, and the games are offered for restore by name.

There is exactly one setting today: the CPU core. auto is the default — the interpreter for real-mode programs, the recompiling (JIT) core for protected-mode ones; normal, dynamic, simple and prefetch are the alternatives, and normal is the fallback for old programs that misbehave on the recompiler. The licence travels with the app: the full GPL v2 text and the NOTICE are inside the APK, and the launcher's footer opens them, next to the source and the privacy policy. The licence screen, inside the APK. The GPL v2 text, the NOTICE and the link to the source, all offline. The Back button works. From Android 13 on the system stopped sending the back key to the app, and SDL's surface swallowed what did arrive, so the button did nothing at all. The app handles it itself now, and the presses walk out in order: the launcher, then Game Mode, then the keyboard panel, then the app. And every loadable segment of libdosbox.so is aligned for 16 KB memory pages, so the library loads on the 64-bit devices that require them — Android 15 and newer.

examples/game-bundle holds STARFALL: a 16-bit DOS arcade game in assembly, about 5 KB, one .COM file, no runtime. It exercises VGA graphics, the BIOS keyboard buffer and the PC speaker, so a new user can install a bundle, press Play and watch something run without finding a game first. STARFALL in the emulator. The keys are the app's, not the game's. The OPL test, running. It holds one tone on the FM chip so that the exact sound snapshot can be proved. examples/opl-test-bundle is a test, not a game: it programs one sustained tone on the FM chip and waits for a key. That is how the exact sound restore is proved — the app writes one line to the log on every save and on every load, and the two have to be identical, two minutes of live chip time apart.
documents.s: STARFALL, and a test that proves the sound

documents.t: The Android migration is finished, and the repository carries a tag that says so: milestone/android-migration-complete The core builds for three ABIs, the app layer works, save states carry the whole machine with the sound chips included. What follows is maintenance: bug fixes and documentation, no new features. The ledger of every release — what each version changed and why — lives in downloads/README.md in the repository. The ones that shaped the app are written up here as stories: DOSBox inside an APK, the whole machine in one file, the keyboard becomes a handheld console, the save that outlives the app and a console-style gamepad for your thumb. The announcement is where this started; the user guide is the step-by-step version, and the interrupt map lists every INT the emulator answers.

Everything is verified on an emulator — API 37, x86_64. There is no real ARM64 run, no on-device benchmark, and no on-device check of the JIT's RWX code cache. That cache is the risk surface on a real phone: if the allocation were refused, DOSBox exits with Allocating dynamic cache failed instead of falling back, and the answer there is core=normal. The audio latency is not tuned yet — the block size and the prebuffer still carry the Emscripten build's numbers. There are no GLES2 scalers, so the picture relies on the CPU scalers. A bundle cannot be exported back out, and one shipping its own dosbox.conf cannot be run yet. There is no real gamepad: the tree references no SDL_CONTROLLER*, and DOSBox still uses the legacy SDL_Joystick. There is no IME and no non-ASCII text input — the keyboard emits key codes, not text. android:allowBackup is still an open product decision: should the DOS files in the private directory be backed up? There is no R8/ProGuard shrinking, and no Play Store AAB from this repository. And some old DOS programs still do not survive a restore — the extender of Ultima VIII, for example — because the snapshot does not capture the DMA controller, the EMS/XMS handle tables and the PIC event queue yet. That is a limitation of the DOS internals, not of the app.

This post is not the manual. The manual is the repository: the README — what the app is, and how the port touches the core; docs/TECHNICAL-REFERENCE.md — the whole implementation in one document; docs/USER-GUIDE.md — the guide for the phone's owner; docs/INTERRUPTS.md — the interrupt map, every INT the emulator answers; docs/PRIVACY.md — the privacy policy, next to COPYING and NOTICE, where its whole history is public. None of this is possible without the DOSBox project. DOSBox was written by the DOSBox Team — a volunteer crew who took an operating system from 1994 and made it runnable on every machine the world has produced since, including the ones that did not exist yet. They kept it alive for three decades and gave it away to anyone who wanted it. WhereQ-DOSBox is a thin layer on top of their work; the originality, the craft and the generosity are entirely theirs. This port is built on Em-DOSBox, the Emscripten build of DOSBox r4305 by Boris Gjenero, which grew out of Ismail Khatib's first attempt to compile DOSBox with Emscripten, and rode on the Emscripten work of Alon Zakai. A phone in your pocket can open a DOS prompt. That is the whole idea, and it took longer than it should have.

A save state is the one thing the emulator exists for. It is the whole machine, frozen — the CPU, the DOS memory, the video memory, the open file handles, the timers — so that you can come back to the exact moment you left. Until this release, that frozen machine lived inside the app's own private storage. Android deletes that storage the moment the app is uninstalled. So it happens the boring way. The phone is full, or the app starts misbehaving, or you simply decide to reinstall it. You install the APK again, the game bundle is still sitting in the folder you picked, you press Play — and the game starts at the very beginning. Ten hours of progress, gone. Not because the game was lost. Because the app was. And a phone that falls in the river takes the app with it, and the app takes the saves with it. That was the truth about WhereQ-DOSBox until 1.0.0.12: the one thing the emulator exists to protect was the one thing that could not survive the app. The save-state sheet. Three slots per game — these are the files that used to die with the app.
documents.s: WhereQ-DOSBox 1.0.0.12: the save that outlives the app

documents.t: The fix is not clever. It is that the saves stop living in a place Android is allowed to delete. Pick a folder on the phone — Config → Saves folder, or the offer that appears after the first save — and every slot is mirrored there, gzipped, right next to the game itself: the app the folder you picked ────── ──────────────────── the slot ── gzip ──▶ STARFALL/ slot1.gz slot2.gz bundle.zip (the game) Now the games are yours, in a folder you chose, and their save states are already there beside them. And that folder is not a special place. It is an ordinary folder in the phone's storage: you can copy it, sync it, move it, put it on a cloud drive — the same way you would treat any other folder of files. One thing to know before you pick it: Android will not let an app take the Download folder itself, because that would be too broad a permission. Pick any other one — Documents is fine.
documents.s: The saves live outside the app now

documents.t: A reinstall, a new phone, an app deleted by accident. The games are offered for restore by name, with their save states already there beside them. The Files panel: the games, and the Config button where the saves folder is set. The same panel after a save. The green line names the game, the slot and the time — a save is a thing with a date on it, not a guess. One detail worth knowing, because it is the kind of thing that quietly loses work: two archives with the same file name are told apart by name — game and game (2) — so their saves never end up in the same place.
documents.s: The games come back by name

documents.t: The second thing in this release is inside the save file, and it is about the mouse. A DOS program does not just read the mouse. It configures it: it registers an event callback, sets the range the cursor may travel in, picks a cursor shape and the hotspot inside that shape, and decides how coarse and how sensitive the movement is. All of that is a property of the game, and the game will never send it again. So a save state has to carry it. 1.0.0.11 carried far too much. It put the whole INT 33h driver into the snapshot — the event queue, the click counters and the interrupt re-entrancy flags included. Restoring that wedged mouse-driven games: the stale queue and the stuck flags fed garbage into the interrupt handler and into the game's own callback, and a game could hang on load. The machine came back, but the mouse never reached the game again. So the snapshot now carries the configuration the guest cannot rebuild itself, and leaves the run-time state out: in the save state not in the save state the game's event-callback registration the queue of pending events the cursor range and position the click counters the cursor shape and its hotspot the interrupt re-entrancy flags the granularity and the sensitivity which buttons were held down The cursor shape matters as much as the rest. Without it the visible cursor reverts to the default block and stops lining up with the real click point, so your taps land beside the target instead of on it. A game that reads the mouse live. This is the kind that used to hang on a restore. What a restore no longer carries is the state of the moment you saved. That belongs to the past, not to the machine you are coming back to. A restored game starts from an idle driver, with the mouse released — if you were holding a button down across the save, you press it again.
documents.s: What a save state should remember

documents.t: Save states written by 1.0.0.11 and by the earlier 1.0.0.12 cuts cannot be loaded by this build. The state file grew a version when the mouse block changed, and an older state is refused rather than misread. That is the honest behaviour — a state that is half understood is worse than a state that is refused — but it does mean those slots are gone.
documents.s: Your old save states will not load

documents.t: The tag still reads v1.0.0.12, but the file behind the download link is a different build than the one first published under that name. Its checksum is a different checksum, too. The one below is the checksum of the file as it is now. If you downloaded this release earlier and compared it, a mismatch is expected.

The package id is still com.whereq.dosbox, the signing key is still the same one, and the download file and the tag still carry the project's own name, so it installs over 1.0.0.11 in place. Nothing to uninstall first, and your games and your slots stay where they are. The project is GPL-2.0, and the DOSBox core is embedded with its AUTHORS, ChangeLog, COPYING and per-file headers intact.

This post is not the manual. The manual is the repository: README says what the app is, docs/TECHNICAL-REFERENCE.md is the whole implementation in one document — the save-state machine and the durable saves folder are both in it — docs/USER-GUIDE.md walks through it step by step, and docs/INTERRUPTS.md is the interrupt map. Please read those rather than take my word for it. The rest of the story is here: DOSBox inside an APK, the whole machine in one file, the keyboard becomes a handheld console, a console-style gamepad for your thumb. The announcement is where this started, and the project today is where it stands. A save that dies with the app is a save you were never really keeping. If your games live in a folder on the phone and their saves do not — this is the release that puts them side by side.

None of this is possible without the DOSBox project. DOSBox was written by the DOSBox Team — a volunteer crew who took an operating system from 1994 and made it runnable on every machine the world has produced since, including the ones that did not exist yet. They kept it alive for three decades and gave it away to anyone who wanted it. WhereQ-DOSBox is a thin layer on top of their work. The originality, the craft and the generosity are entirely theirs. This port is built on Em-DOSBox, the Emscripten build of DOSBox r4305 by Boris Gjenero, which grew out of Ismail Khatib's first attempt to compile DOSBox with Emscripten, and rode on the Emscripten work of Alon Zakai. The SDL2 library by Sam Lantinga carries the window, the audio and the touch input. DOSBox is a trademark of the DOSBox project; this port is not affiliated with or endorsed by the DOSBox team.

存档是这个模拟器存在的理由。它把整台机器冻住——CPU、DOS 内存、显存、打开的文件句柄、硬件定时器——让你能回到离开的那一刻。 在这一版之前，这台冻住的机器住在应用自己的私有目录里。而 Android 会在你卸载应用的那一刻，把那个目录一起删掉。 于是事情往往是这样发生的：手机存储满了，或者应用开始出怪问题，或者你只是想重装一遍。你重新装上 APK，游戏压缩包还在你选的那个文件夹里，你按下 Play——游戏却从第一关开始了。 十个小时的进度没了。不是因为游戏丢了，而是因为应用没了。 手机掉进河里，也是同一个道理：应用没了，存档跟着没了。 在 1.0.0.12 之前，WhereQ-DOSBox 的处境就是这样：这个模拟器唯一存在的理由保不住。 存档面板。每个游戏三个档位——以前跟着应用一起没命的就是这些文件。

修法并不复杂：存档不再待在 Android 可以随手删掉的地方。 在手机上选一个文件夹——Config → Saves folder，或者第一次存档之后弹出来的那句询问——之后每个档位都会镜像到那里，压成 gzip，就放在游戏旁边： 应用 你选的那个文件夹 ────── ──────────────────── 存档 ── gzip ──▶ STARFALL/ slot1.gz slot2.gz bundle.zip (游戏本身) 于是游戏归你了，在你自己挑的文件夹里，它们的存档也已经躺在旁边。 而且这个文件夹并不是什么特殊的地方。它就是手机存储里一个普普通通的文件夹：可以复制、可以同步、可以搬家、可以丢进网盘，跟你对待任何一个装着文件的文件夹没有区别。选之前有一件事要知道：Android 不允许应用直接占用 Download 这个目录，那权限太宽了。挑别的就行——Documents 就很好。

重装、换手机、手滑删了应用——游戏会按名字出现在恢复列表里，它们的存档已经在旁边等着了。 Files 面板：游戏列表，以及设置存档目录的 Config 按钮。 存过一次之后的同一个面板。绿色那一行把游戏、档位和时间都写了出来——存档是个有日期的东西，不靠猜。 有个细节值得知道，因为它是那种悄悄弄丢进度的东西：同名的两个压缩包会按名字区分——game 和 game (2)——所以它们的存档不会混到同一个地方去。

这一版的另一件事在存档文件内部，说的是鼠标。 DOS 程序不只是读鼠标，它还要配置鼠标：注册事件回调，规定光标能走到的范围，选一个光标形状和形状里的热点，再决定移动有多粗、有多敏感。这些都是游戏的属性，而游戏自己不会再发一遍。所以存档必须带着它们。 1.0.0.11 带得太多了。它把整个 INT 33h 驱动塞进了快照——事件队列、点击计数、中断重入标志全都在内。读回这样的快照，靠鼠标操作的游戏就卡死了：过期的队列和卡住的标志会把乱七八糟的东西塞进中断处理程序，塞进游戏自己的回调，读档时游戏可能直接挂住。机器回来了，鼠标却再也送不到游戏手里。 所以现在，快照只带着程序自己重建不出来的那部分配置，把运行时的状态留在外面： 存档里有的 存档里没有的 游戏注册的事件回调 排着队等处理的事件 光标的范围和当前位置 点击计数器 光标的形状和热点 中断重入标志 粒度和灵敏度 当时按着哪些键 光标的形状和别的同样重要。少了它，屏幕上那个光标会退回默认的方块，不再和真正的点击位置对齐，于是你的手指点在了目标旁边，而不是目标上。 一款实时读鼠标的游戏。以前读档就可能让它挂在这里。 读档不再带回来的，是存档那一刻的运行状态。那属于过去，不属于你要回来的这台机器。读档之后，游戏从鼠标松开的状态重新开始——如果你存档时正按着某个键，读完档要再按一次。
1.0.0.11 以及更早那几个 1.0.0.12 切出来的存档，这一版读不了。 鼠标那一块改了之后，存档文件的版本也跟着长了一版，老存档会被拒绝，而不是被误读。这样做是诚实的——只读懂一半的存档，比读不出来的存档更糟——但这也意味着那些档位确实没了。
标签还是 v1.0.0.12，但下载链接后面那个文件，和最初用这个名字发布的那一个不是同一个构建，校验和自然也不一样。下面这个校验和是当前这个文件的。如果你在更早的时候下载过这一版，发现对不上，那是预期之中的。

发布版 APK 在发布页上，用项目自己的发布证书签名： 👉 github.com/whereq/whereq-dosbox — tag v1.0.0.12 whereq-dosbox-1.0.0.12.apk size: 16 536 964 bytes (15.8 MB) sha256: 67577d59e078cd2953c24ea24753068aae2a01c2cf27a9788644787e999f2fd9 APK 本身在这里：whereq-dosbox-1.0.0.12.apk —— 签名证书的 SHA-256 是 b16b480d5a1ff6d35baff0b15fa3fc4b0ee815e500861fbff1b062c9bf7d3933。 要装这一版的人注意一件事：这一版在手机上的名字是 A-DOS——Android 和 Apple 上的 DOS。包名还是 com.whereq.dosbox，签名密钥还是原来那一个，下载文件名和标签也仍然是项目自己的，所以它可以直接覆盖安装 1.0.0.11，不用先卸载，你的游戏和档位都原地不动。 它跑在 arm64-v8a、armeabi-v7a 和 x86_64 设备上，要求 Android 5.0 及以上，完全离线，不需要账号，也没有任何追踪。项目采用 GPL-2.0 许可，DOSBox 核心连同它的 AUTHORS、ChangeLog、COPYING 和逐文件的头注释一起嵌入。

这篇文章不是手册。手册是仓库本身：README 讲这个应用是什么；docs/TECHNICAL-REFERENCE.md 是整个实现写在一份文档里——存档机器和那个「活过应用」的存档目录都在里面；docs/USER-GUIDE.md 一步一步带着你走一遍；docs/INTERRUPTS.md 是中断地图。请去读那些，而不是信我的一面之词。 故事的其他几段在这里：装进 APK 的 DOSBox、整台机器，装进一个文件、把键盘改造成掌机、给拇指一个掌机。公告是这一切的起点，项目的今天是它现在的位置。 跟着应用一起没命的存档，本来就不是你真正留下的存档。如果你的游戏在手机上的某个文件夹里，而它们的存档不在——这一版会把两者放到一起。

没有 DOSBox 项目，这一切都不可能。 DOSBox 由 DOSBox Team 写成——一群志愿者把 1994 年的一套操作系统改造到此后世界造出的每一台机器上都能跑，包括那些当时还不存在的机器。他们让它活过了三十年，并免费交给任何想要的人。WhereQ-DOSBox 只是建在他们工作之上的一层薄薄的壳。原创力、手艺和慷慨完全属于他们。 这个移植基于 Em-DOSBox——Boris Gjenero 做的 DOSBox r4305 的 Emscripten 版，它又来自 Ismail Khatib 最早那次用 Emscripten 编译 DOSBox 的尝试，并且踩着 Alon Zakai 的 Emscripten 工作一路往前。窗口、音频和触摸输入则由 Sam Lantinga 的 SDL2 库承担。 DOSBox 是 DOSBox 项目的商标；这个移植与 DOSBox 团队没有任何隶属或背书关系。

There is a moment in every DOS game played on a phone where the game stops being a game and becomes a dexterity test. You are holding the phone in two hands, and the game wants three things at once: go left, fire, jump. The on-screen keyboard is a good way to type MOUNT C . and a bad way to play that. One thumb stays on the arrows; the other one has to leave them to find the letter B, and for a second — a second that a game with a timer does not give you — nobody is steering. So you play the games you can finish with one thumb, and you do not play the others. A keyboard built for typing is a fine typewriter and a poor controller. 1.0.0.15 gives that keyboard a second face. The keyboard pads in landscape: the picture in the middle, one hand on each side. This is the layout Game Mode replaces.
documents.s: One thumb was never going to be enough

documents.t: Game Mode lives inside the keyboard panel. There is no second app to open: the phone simply grows a different set of controls in the same place. With the keyboard pads showing, switch Caps Lock on — double-tap Shift if you would rather not hunt for it — and type the code already in everybody's fingers: ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A The pads flip. What was a QWERTY board becomes an eight-way D-pad, a trackball, and the buttons a DOS game actually fires, jumps and strafes with: Y, X, CTRL, ALT, SPACE and ENT. The D-pad is the part you will use most, and the part you will press hardest: eight directions under one thumb, nothing to reach for. The trackball takes the other thumb and moves the pointer like a laptop touchpad — stroke to move, tap to click. The Hybrid profile: a D-pad on the left, a trackball on the right, and the mouse buttons beside it. The gold button at the top-left names the profile, and each game remembers the one you last used with it. Hybrid is the default — a D-pad and a trackball, for the games that mix keys and mouse. Action swaps the trackball for the buttons a keyboard arcade game actually wants: FIRE, JUMP, USE and ENT. Point & click goes the other way, with big LEFT and RIGHT mouse buttons under the left thumb. The Action profile: FIRE, JUMP, USE and ENT, for the games that fire and jump on the keyboard. The Point & click profile: the mouse buttons take the whole left pad, the trackball the right one. To go back, type the same code on the D-pad and then X, Y — the face buttons stand in for B and A. Or press the phone's Back button, which leaves Game Mode as readily as it leaves the keyboard.
documents.s: The pads turn into a gamepad

documents.t: The code is matched on the case the letters are actually typed in. That sounds like pedantry, and it is not. Type a lowercase "ba" and the emulator does exactly what you asked: it types "ba" into the DOS prompt, and you sit at C:\> with two stray letters and a game that never started. So the B and the A must be capital. Caps Lock is not a suggestion — it is the first half of the spell.
documents.s: The two letters that have to be capital

documents.t: DOS games do not agree on what "up" is: some read the cursor keys, some the numeric keypad, and the ones written after the letters became a game input read WASD. The button under the D-pad cycles between the three, and the app remembers your choice per game: mode up / down / left / right a diagonal pick it for ARROWS the arrow keys ↑ ↓ ← → two keys at once (↑ + →) most games — anything that reads the cursor keys NUMPAD the keypad 8 / 2 / 4 / 6 a single key — 7 / 9 / 1 / 3 keypad games, where a diagonal is a key of its own WASD the letters W / A / S / D two keys at once (W + D) later shooters, and anything mapped to WASD The button carries the name of the mode you actually have, so it never says ARROWS while the pad is sending WASD. And if your game ignores the D-pad, it is almost always the wrong mode — switch until it answers.

Every game wants its buttons somewhere else. The one that shoots on X and the one that shoots on Y are both common, and both are wrong for you at least once. Long-press the gold profile button and pick Remap buttons…. The screen enters remap mode: the buttons that can be changed are outlined in gold, you tap one, a list of keys opens, and you pick the key you would rather have. Long-press the gold profile button and the picker opens — the three profiles, and the way into the remap screen. Remap mode: the gold outline marks the buttons you can change; on the gold FIRE button it has to be dark brown, or it would disappear. The remap belongs to that one game and is remembered: the same title always plays the same way, next time and the next.

Here is the part I am happiest about, and it is not a feature you can see. The gamepad pushes the same SDL key events the on-screen keyboard pushes, and they travel the same road: through the mapper, into the emulated keyboard, into the BIOS buffer, out through INT 09h like a real keystroke. The guest cannot tell the two apart. There is no new input path to teach a game and no new driver for a 1994 title to be suspicious of. A button on the gamepad is a keystroke, exactly as a key on the keyboard is. That is also why the gamepad asked nothing of the emulator core: it is an app-layer thing, and the core was never told. The mouse is a separate road: the trackball's motion becomes a relative mouse-motion event, the kind a real mouse sends, and the SDL layer now accepts it. The click buttons become real mouse buttons. That is the whole design. The keyboard grew a second skin instead of becoming a new machine. One thing this is not: a joystick. There is no analogue stick behind it and no joystick hardware anywhere in the app — a game that needs a real analogue axis is still a game this app cannot play. STARFALL in the emulator. The pads beside it are still the keyboard ones — in Game Mode they turn into the gamepad in the same place.

The save-state format did not change. Game Mode is a new way of pressing the same keys, so every save state written by the earlier releases loads normally. This one matters more than the feature does. A release that quietly changes the format leaves a generation of slots unopenable; the honest way to change a format is to change it loudly, with a version bump. Three slots per game, a file on the phone behind each of them — the whole machine in one file, as 1.0.0.8 put it.

A smaller fix, in the same release. A shutdown that failed used to abort the process with SIGABRT — and it did that while it was only shutting down, a strange time to crash. The error is caught now and the exit carries on. I would not put this in a headline. But an emulator that dies on the way out teaches you to distrust it, and I would rather it simply left.

The release is on the releases page as tag v1.0.0.15. The APK is published as a release asset built by CI from that tag, with a .sha256 sidecar next to it, so you can check what you downloaded. 👉 github.com/whereq/whereq-dosbox — the source, and the whole history of it. It runs on arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x86_64 devices, Android 5.0 and newer, entirely offline, with no account and no tracking. The project is GPL-2.0, and the DOSBox core is embedded with its AUTHORS, ChangeLog, COPYING and per-file headers intact. If you are new here, the announcement says what the project is, and the user guide walks through every screen of it. The console that the keyboard became is about the pads Game Mode replaces, and the save that outlives the app about the slots that still load. For the whole picture of the project, read WhereQ-DOSBox; for what a key does inside the machine, the interrupt map has it. Again, this post is not the documentation. The documentation is the repository: the Game Mode chapter of the user guide, the technical reference, and the interrupt map. Please read those rather than take my word for it.

None of this is possible without the DOSBox project. DOSBox was written by the DOSBox Team — a volunteer crew who took an operating system from 1994 and made it runnable on every machine the world has produced since, including the ones that did not exist yet. They kept it alive for three decades and gave it away to anyone who wanted it. WhereQ-DOSBox is a thin layer on top of their work, and Game Mode is a thin layer on top of that. The originality, the craft and the generosity are entirely theirs. This port is built on Em-DOSBox, the Emscripten build of DOSBox r4305 by Boris Gjenero, which grew out of Ismail Khatib's first attempt to compile DOSBox with Emscripten, and rode on the Emscripten work of Alon Zakai. The SDL2 library by Sam Lantinga carries the window, the audio and the touch input — and now the gamepad too. DOSBox is a trademark of the DOSBox project; this port is not affiliated with or endorsed by the DOSBox team. A thumb can hold a direction, a button and a ball at the same time. The game, written in 1994, never has to know the difference.

在手机上玩 DOS 游戏，总有那么一个瞬间：游戏不再像游戏，倒像一场手指的杂技。 你双手捧着手机，游戏却同时要你做三件事：向左，开火，跳跃。屏幕键盘拿来敲 MOUNT C . 很顺手，拿来玩游戏就很难受——一只拇指按在方向键上，另一只必须离开方向键去够字母 B，就那么一两秒，而带计时的游戏不会给你这一两秒。 于是你只挑那些单手能玩的游戏；那些要一只手按住方向、另一只手开火的作品，你干脆不碰。为打字而生的键盘，打字足够好，当手柄却不够。 1.0.0.15 给这块键盘添了第二张脸。 横屏时的按键布局：画面在中间，两只手各管一边。Game Mode 要替换的就是 这一套。

Game Mode 就住在键盘面板里，不用再开一个应用，也不用插什么线：手机在同一个位置，换了一套控制。 键盘显示着的时候，打开 Caps Lock（不想找它，双击 Shift 就行），然后敲一段人人都已经存在手指里的暗号： ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A 按键翻面了。原来的 QWERTY 变成一个八向方向键、一颗轨迹球，外加 DOS 游戏真正用来开火、跳跃和横移的那几个键：Y、X、CTRL、ALT、SPACE 和 ENT。 方向键是你用得最多的，也是你会按得最狠的：八个方向，一根拇指，不用够。轨迹球归另一根拇指，像笔记本触控板那样移动——划一下动一点，轻点就是点击。 Hybrid 档案：左边是 D-pad，右边是轨迹球，旁边还有两个鼠标键。 左上角那个金色按钮写着当前的档案，每个游戏都记住你上次和它一起用的那一个。Hybrid 是默认档——D-pad 加轨迹球，给那些既要键又要鼠标的游戏。Action 把轨迹球换成键盘街机游戏真正想要的键：FIRE、JUMP、USE 和 ENT。Point & click 反过来，左拇指下面是大大的 LEFT 和 RIGHT 鼠标键。 Action 档案：FIRE、JUMP、USE 和 ENT，给那些用键盘开火和跳跃的游戏。 Point & click 档案：鼠标键占满左半边，轨迹球占右半边。 要退出来，在方向键上敲同一段暗号，然后按 X、Y，这两个面部键替 B 和 A 上场；或者按手机的返回键，它退出 Game Mode 和退出键盘一样干脆。
这段暗号，是按字母实际打出来的大小写来匹配的。 听着像吹毛求疵，其实不是：你打一个小写的 "ba"，模拟器就老老实实照做，把 "ba" 打进了 DOS 提示符。你坐在 C:\> 面前，屏幕上多出两个莫名其妙的字母，游戏根本没开始。 所以 B 和 A 必须是大写。Caps Lock 不是建议，是这段咒语的前半句。

DOS 游戏对「上」这个方向各说各话：有的读方向键，有的读数字小键盘——在小键盘那里，斜向本身就是一个键；等字母也能当操作键之后写出来的游戏，则读 WASD。 方向键下面那个按钮就在三种模式之间轮换，应用会按游戏记住你选的那一种： 模式 上 / 下 / 左 / 右 斜向 适合 ARROWS 方向键 ↑ ↓ ← → 同时按两个键（↑ + →） 大多数游戏——凡是读方向键的 NUMPAD 小键盘 8 / 2 / 4 / 6 单个键——7 / 9 / 1 / 3 按小键盘做的游戏，斜向自成一个键 WASD 字母 W / A / S / D 同时按两个键（W + D） 后来的射击游戏，以及一切绑定了 WASD 的游戏 按钮上写的就是你当前实际用的那个模式，不会一边写着 ARROWS、一边发的是 WASD。如果游戏完全不理方向键，八成是模式不对——换到它有反应为止。

每个游戏都想把按钮放在自己顺手的地方。有的用 X 开火，有的用 Y，都很常见，而且多半都不合你的手。 长按那个金色的档案按钮，选 Remap buttons…。屏幕进入映射模式：可以改的按钮镀着一圈金色描边，你点其中一个，弹出一串按键，选你更想要的那个。 长按那个金色的档案按钮，选择器就弹出来——三个档案，以及进入映射页面的入口。 映射模式。金色描边标出的是可以改的键；在金色的 FIRE 按钮上，描边得是深 褐色，否则就看不见了。 这套映射属于这一个游戏，并且会被记住：同一个游戏下次打开，还是老样子。

下面这件事看不见，却是我自己最满意的部分。 手柄推上去的 SDL 按键事件，和屏幕键盘推上去的完全一样，走的也是同一条路：经过 mapper，进模拟键盘，进 BIOS 缓冲区，最后像一次真正的击键那样从 INT 09h 送出去。运行在 DOS 里的程序分辨不出两者的区别。没有一条新的输入通路需要游戏去学，也没有新的驱动需要 1994 年的游戏去提防。手柄上的一个按钮就是一个按键，跟键盘上的一个键没有区别。 这也是为什么这个手柄没向模拟器核心要任何东西：它是应用层的事，核心从头到尾都不知道它存在。 鼠标走的是另一条路：轨迹球的移动会变成相对位移的鼠标事件，和真实鼠标发的那种一样，SDL 这一层现在接受它们；点击按钮则是真正的鼠标按钮。 整个设计就是这样：键盘长出了第二层皮，而不是变成了另一台机器。 有一点它不是：它不是摇杆。背后没有模拟摇杆，应用里也根本没有手柄硬件——需要真正模拟轴的游戏，这个应用照样玩不了。 模拟器里跑着的 STARFALL。画面两边的还是键盘的按键——进了 Game Mode， 它们在同一个位置变成手柄。
存档格式什么都没改。 Game Mode 只是换了一种按同样的键的方式，所以之前各版本写下的存档都照常读得出来。 这一条比功能本身还重要。一次悄悄改掉格式的发布，会留下一批再也打不开的存档；老实做法是——格式真变了就大声改，带版本号地改。 每个游戏三个槽位，每个槽位背后是手机上的一个文件——整台机器装进一个 文件，1.0.0.8 干的就是这件事。
同一版里还带了一个小修复。 以前关机的过程中一旦出错，进程会被 SIGABRT 直接打死——偏偏是在它自己正准备退出的那一刻崩掉，这个时机很怪。现在这个错误会被接住，退出流程照常走完。 这件事我不会写进标题。但一个退出时都会死掉的模拟器，会让人开始不信任它；我更希望它只是安安静静地走掉。

这一版在发布页上，tag 是 v1.0.0.15。APK 由 CI 从这个 tag 构建，作为发布资产传上去，旁边还放着一个 .sha256 文件，下载下来可以自己核对。 👉 github.com/whereq/whereq-dosbox ——源代码，以及它全部的来历。 它跑在 arm64-v8a、armeabi-v7a 和 x86_64 设备上，要求 Android 5.0 及以上，完全离线，不需要账号，也没有任何追踪。项目采用 GPL-2.0 许可，DOSBox 核心连同它的 AUTHORS、ChangeLog、COPYING 和逐文件头注释一起嵌入。 刚认识这个项目的话，公告 说的是它是什么，用户手册 带你走过每一个界面；把键盘改造成掌机 讲的是 Game Mode 要替换掉的那两块按键区，活过应用的存档 讲的是那些至今还读得出来的存档。项目现在的整体状态，看 WhereQ-DOSBox；一个按键进了机器之后发生了什么，看中断表。 再说一次：这篇文章不是文档。 文档是仓库本身：用户手册 里的 Game Mode 一章、技术参考，还有中断表。请去读那些，而不是信我的一面之词。

没有 DOSBox 项目，这一切都不可能。 DOSBox 由 DOSBox Team 写成——一群志愿者把 1994 年的一套操作系统改造到此后世界造出的每一台机器上都能跑，包括那些当时还不存在的机器。他们让它活过了三十年，并免费交给任何想要的人。WhereQ-DOSBox 只是建在他们工作之上的一层薄壳，Game Mode 不过是那层壳上的另一层。原创力、手艺和慷慨完全属于他们。 这个移植基于 Em-DOSBox——Boris Gjenero 做的 DOSBox r4305 的 Emscripten 版，它又来自 Ismail Khatib 最早那次用 Emscripten 编译 DOSBox 的尝试，并且踩着 Alon Zakai 的 Emscripten 工作一路往前。窗口、音频和触摸输入由 Sam Lantinga 的 SDL2 库承担——现在手柄也归它管，毕竟一路到底都是同一批事件。 DOSBox 是 DOSBox 项目的商标；这个移植与 DOSBox 团队没有任何隶属或背书关系。 一根拇指可以同时按住一个方向、一个键和一颗球。而那款写于 1994 年的游戏，永远不需要知道这中间的差别。

Somewhere in most houses there is a Bluetooth keyboard. It came with a tablet, or a phone, or a television, and it has been sitting in a drawer ever since — a rectangle of plastic with a hundred and four keys that feel better than anything a screen can pretend to be. Pair it with the phone and it works. For everything. Except the emulator. That was the state of WhereQ-DOSBox until this release: you paired the keyboard, you pressed a key, and nothing happened. Not "the wrong key" — nothing. The vendored SDL2 has no path for Android key events at all; the Java layer fed only the IME, and the native side never saw a single key event come in. The on-screen keyboard was the only input the app had, and a game that wanted a keypress got a finger instead. 1.0.0.18 fixes that, and it fixes it the way the app does everything else: by refusing to invent a new input path. An Android key code is now mapped to a DOSBox key name, and that name is resolved through the same native table the on-screen keyboard already used. Both roads end in the same scancode, in the same BIOS buffer, behind the same INT 09h. Shift, Ctrl and Alt are carried along, so DOS sees the capital letters it should. Only the first press of a held key is forwarded — DOSBox does its own auto-repeat in the BIOS timer, and every extra event would be one more scancode in the buffer. And a keystroke aimed at the launch-script editor never reaches the game, which is the one thing that had to stay true. Checked in the emulator with real key events, not with a mock: the letters and Enter pass the copy protection of Mortal Kombat, F1 starts the game, F10 opens its own options menu, and the arrow keys move the menu cursor and are accepted as the game's movement keys. The keyboard in the drawer is a DOS keyboard now.

There was a note that the emulator added to some games. Not in the music — on top of it: a steady beat, a warble that rode along under the soundtrack and vanished the moment you turned the music off. It was the most annoying kind of bug, because it was partly true. The tone was really there. It was also really not supposed to be there, and no amount of listening could separate the two. The cause is a piece of arithmetic in the mixer, and it took a diagram to explain. DOSBox keeps its audio buffer centred by continuously re-tuning the emulator's effective output sample rate: the producer thread runs on the emulated PIT's clock, the consumer thread runs on the phone's audio clock, and the two never agree exactly, so on every callback the mixer nudges the rate to keep the buffer near its set point. That is a fine design on a desktop. Under the steady, heavy load of OPL/FM synthesis on a phone, though, the loop hunts. And a held FM note is a sustained carrier — exactly the kind of signal that turns a wandering sample rate into an audible beat. The digital sound effects, being transient, never revealed it: they were too short to sit on a warble. The test that exposed it: one sustained tone on the FM chip — the carrier that a wandering sample rate turns into a beat. The fix is three lines in the dosbox.conf the app ships: the mixer runs at 48 kHz, the phone's native rate, in blocks of 2048, with a 50 ms prebuffer. The loop stops hunting, and the warble goes with it. This changes audio buffering and nothing else. Game speed and logic are untouched, and the price is about 50 ms of latency, which is inaudible in a DOS game. The whole analysis — the pipeline, the control loop, the modulation — is in docs/AUDIO-FM-BEEP.md, with three diagrams, because the interesting part of this bug was never the three lines.
documents.s: A tone that was never in the music

documents.t: Leaving the app with the Back button and opening it again used to be enough to kill the emulator. DOS:Too many devices added The device table is a static array of ten slots, and the devices of a run were never removed from it. The app keeps its process alive between two starts, so the second start found the table still full, ran out of slots and died. The devices of the DOS section are now removed when it shuts down; the MSCDEX device removes itself with it.

Two smaller fixes in the same corner of the app. The gamepad restores your per-game state — the profile, the D-pad mode, the remaps — in one pass now, before the gamepad is built. The order mattered: the D-pad has to be in place before the bar is built, or the chip that names the mode names the previous one, and the separate setters had to be called in an order the caller could get wrong. One layout pass cannot get it wrong. And the TURBO auto-fire cannot get stuck any more. While the FIRE button is held, TURBO fires it again and again. That loop lived in the button's own touch listener, and a rebuild — a rotation, or the other thumb cycling a chip — detached the view mid-hold without an ACTION_UP. The listener never stopped, and the key fired forever. The loop now lives with the gamepad, and every path that releases the keys cancels it.
documents.s: Game Mode comes back the way you left it

documents.t: The columns layout: one key column per side, for the screen where the pads no longer fit. The user guide had described the keyboard's three layouts and pictured two of them. The third — the columns layout, one key column per side, that the app falls back to when the black bar beside the 4:3 picture drops below 116 dp — is now a real capture, as is the narrow landscape screen where the letters are squeezed to about 24 dp. The new Game Mode screenshots were re-taken from the 1.0.0.17 release build, so the frames in the guide, in the repository and in the capture set are the same ones. The dead SEE ALSO section is out of the DOSBox man page, the remap outline is checked on the device in pixels, and the checksum of the shipped 1.0.0.17 APK is recorded in the repository.

The save-state format did not change. Every save state written by the earlier releases loads normally. Nothing in this release touches the emulator's internals — it is an app-layer release, like the ones before it — but this is the sentence that has to be in every release note, so here it is again.

DOSBox was written by the DOSBox Team — a volunteer crew who took an operating system from 1994 and made it runnable on every machine the world has produced since, including the ones that did not exist yet. They kept it alive for three decades and gave it away to anyone who wanted it. WhereQ-DOSBox is a thin layer on top of their work, and this release is a thin layer on top of that. The originality, the craft and the generosity are entirely theirs. This port is built on Em-DOSBox, the Emscripten build of DOSBox r4305 by Boris Gjenero, which grew out of Ismail Khatib's first attempt to compile DOSBox with Emscripten, and rode on the Emscripten work of Alon Zakai.
